fields.title: Portraits of Courage – C. S. Lewis
fields.subtitle: A Promise Kept, a Reluctant Convert, and a Late and Costly Love
fields.description: A Christian biography of C. S. Lewis (1898–1963), the Belfast boy who lost his mother and his faith, survived the trenches, kept a dead friend’s promise for thirty years, and came by way of Addison’s Walk to Christ. It follows him through the Kilns, the Inklings, the wartime broadcasts, Narnia and Cambridge to his marriage to Joy Davidman and A Grief Observed. An independent Ochorus life, not endorsed by the Lewis estate; all Scripture from the public-domain King James Version.
fields.about_html:
This is a biography of C. S. Lewis, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus as the seventh volume of Portraits of Courage, it tells his whole life in narrative: the Belfast childhood and the mother he lost at nine; the schools he hated and the atheist tutor he loved; the trenches of 1918 and the promise he made to a friend who did not come home; thirty years in the household of that friend’s mother; three firsts and a fellowship at Magdalen; the long, reluctant road from atheism to God and then to Christ, by way of Addison’s Walk and a sidecar to Whipsnade; the Kilns, the Inklings and Charles Williams; the wartime broadcasts and the talks to airmen; weekly confession, daily prayer, the Agape Fund and thousands of letters answered by hand; the Socratic Club and the Anscombe debate; Narnia and Cambridge; his marriage to Joy Davidman, twice, and her death; A Grief Observed; and his own death at home on 22 November 1963.

It is an independent work. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by the C. S. Lewis estate or by any company that holds rights in his writings. Lewis’s own books are still in copyright and should be obtained from their publishers. This book tells his life in its own words, quotes him only in three short sentences, each with its source, and does not retell his stories. His teaching is set out in a separate Ochorus companion, Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis.

Where the sources disagree, on the year he came to believe in God, on the nature of his relationship with Janie Moore, or on what happened at the Socratic Club in 1948, the book says so and gives the main views fairly. It is written with gratitude but not hagiography, naming real struggles: his pride, his deception of his father, his brother’s alcoholism and his own grief. All Scripture is from the King James Version. It ends with lessons from his life, a study guide, a chronology, and a note on sources with further reading, including the public-domain classics he loved that are in the Ochorus library: Athanasius, Augustine, Bunyan, Thomas à Kempis and William Law.

qa.question: What is this biography of C. S. Lewis about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of C. S. Lewis (1898–1963), the Oxford and Cambridge scholar who came from atheism to faith in Christ in 1931. It follows his whole life: his Belfast childhood and his mother’s death, the trenches of the First World War, thirty years in the household of Janie Moore, his conversion, the Inklings, the wartime broadcasts, Narnia, his late marriage to Joy Davidman, her death, and his own.

qa.question: Who was C. S. Lewis?
qa.answer: Clive Staples Lewis, known as Jack, was born in Belfast in 1898. He was a Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, for nearly thirty years and then Professor of Medieval and Renaissance English at Cambridge. After returning to the Christian faith he became its best-known defender in the English-speaking world, through radio talks, books such as Mere Christianity and The Screwtape Letters, and the seven Chronicles of Narnia.

qa.question: Is this book connected with the C. S. Lewis estate?
qa.answer: No. It is an independent biography, not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by the C. S. Lewis estate or by any company that holds rights in his works. Lewis’s books are still in copyright and should be obtained from their publishers. This book tells his life in its own words and quotes him only in three short sentences, each with its source.

qa.question: How does this book differ from Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis?
qa.answer: Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis sets out what he taught: joy, the moral law, pain, prayer, the four loves and glory. This book is a narrative life. It tells what happened to him and to the people around him, and touches his ideas only where they are part of the story.

qa.question: When did C. S. Lewis become a Christian?
qa.answer: In two steps. He came to believe in God alone in his rooms at Magdalen, a moment he dated to 1929 but which most scholars now place in 1930. He came to believe in Christ in September 1931, after a long night talk with J. R. R. Tolkien and Hugo Dyson on Addison’s Walk on 19 September, and a ride to Whipsnade Zoo in his brother’s sidecar nine days later.

qa.question: What was the relationship between C. S. Lewis and Mrs Moore?
qa.answer: Janie Moore was the mother of Paddy Moore, a friend Lewis made in army training, who was killed in 1918. The two young men had promised to care for each other’s families, and Lewis lived with and supported Mrs Moore from 1919 until her death in 1951. Whether they were lovers in the early years is disputed; the book sets out the views and does not claim to know.

qa.question: Why did C. S. Lewis marry Joy Davidman twice?
qa.answer: In April 1956 he married her in a civil ceremony so that she could stay in England, regarding it as a formality. When she was found to have cancer that autumn, he realised that he loved her. The Bishop of Oxford refused a church wedding because she was divorced, and on 21 March 1957 a priest, Peter Bide, married them at her hospital bedside and prayed for her healing. She recovered for three years and died on 13 July 1960.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the King James Version that carries its theme, beginning with Romans 10:20, God found by those who did not seek him. Further passages are woven through the story, and the appendices include lessons from his life, a chapter-by-chapter study guide and a chronology.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me.”

— Romans 10:20, KJV

The earlier volumes of this series told of a Chinese church leader who died in a Communist labour camp, an American who prayed his way through the villages of the Punjab, a Dutch watchmaker who hid Jews behind a false wall, a Scottish mill girl who went alone up the rivers of Calabar, an African bishop who had once been sold as a slave, and an Indian widow who built a home for thousands of outcast women. This seventh volume tells the story of a man whose courage looked much less dramatic than any of theirs. He was never imprisoned for his faith. He never went to a mission field. He spent nearly all his working life in two of the most comfortable universities in the world, teaching young men to read old poems.

C. S. Lewis is, even so, a portrait of courage. It took courage of an unusual kind to be converted at all, against the grain of his own temper and of the clever company he kept. It took courage to keep, for more than thirty years, a promise made to a friend who was killed in France. It took courage to speak plainly about Christ on the radio to a nation at war, and to go on speaking when the colleagues whose good opinion he valued thought it vulgar. It took courage to marry a dying woman in a hospital ward against the advice of nearly everyone, and more courage still to write down, without disguise, what her death did to his faith. And it took a quieter, daily courage to answer by hand the letters of thousands of strangers, to go to confession every week, and to give away most of what his books earned.

What This Book Is

This book is a narrative life. It follows Lewis from his birth in Belfast in 1898 to his death in Oxford in 1963, and it tries to give the people around him their due: his father Albert, his mother Flora, his brother Warren, the friend called Paddy Moore and Paddy’s mother Janie, J. R. R. Tolkien and the other Inklings, Charles Williams, the priest who heard his confessions, and Joy Davidman, the American poet whom he married twice. It is not an account of his teaching. A companion volume in the Ochorus library, Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis, sets out what he believed and wrote about joy, the moral law, pain, prayer, love and glory. The present book touches his ideas only where they are part of the story of his life, and then only briefly. Nor does it retell his stories. Readers who want Narnia, Screwtape or the planets should go to his own books.

A Word About His Words

That is not only a matter of arrangement. Lewis’s books are still in copyright, they are still in print, and the people who hold the rights in them guard them carefully, as they are entitled to do. This book is an independent Ochorus biography. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by the C. S. Lewis estate or by any company that holds rights in his writings. It tells his life in its own words. Apart from three very short sentences, each given with its source, it does not quote him, and where it reports what he thought or felt it does so in paraphrase. His books are named so that readers can find them, and readers are warmly encouraged to buy them or borrow them from a library and to hear him for themselves. No summary can replace the clarity, the humour and the warmth of the man himself.

Why Courage?

There is a temptation, writing about Lewis, to make him more comfortable than he was. He has become a kind of patron saint for Christians who like books, and his face appears on mugs and calendars. But the man who emerges from his letters, from his brother’s diaries and from the memories of those who knew him was not comfortable. He was proud and knew it. He could be overbearing in argument and wounding in his wit. He lost his mother as a child and never really reached his father. He lived for three decades in a household many of his friends found baffling, and some of them found it unhappy. His brother was an alcoholic. His wife died little more than four years after their wedding, and cancer shadowed nearly all of those years. He knew years of exhaustion, and he faced his own death with a mixture of calm and weariness. He was, in short, a sinner who was being made a saint, and the making was slow.

That is what makes his life worth telling. It is the story of a man God pursued for a long time, who resisted for as long as he could, who gave in with very bad grace, and who then spent the rest of his life trying, with all his gifts and all his faults, to serve the One who had caught him.

How This Book Is Written

Like the earlier volumes, this book tries to be honest about its sources. Lewis told part of his own story in Surprised by Joy (1955), but that book is selective by design, and in places his memory can be shown to have slipped. His letters, published in three large volumes, and his brother’s diaries give a fuller and sometimes different picture. Biographers have weighed the evidence carefully, and on a few points they still disagree. Where they do, this book says so and gives the main views fairly. It does not invent dialogue, and it does not put thoughts into anyone’s head that the sources do not support.

Scripture in This Book

Following the companion volume on his teaching, and the Bible Lewis himself grew up with, all Scripture in this book is quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme.

The verse at the head of this preface is Paul’s quotation of Isaiah: God was found by those who did not seek him. Lewis would have said that it was the truest sentence anyone could write about his life. He did not go looking for God. For years he did everything he could to avoid him. But he was found, and the finding changed not only him but millions of people who would never meet him. This book is the story of how that happened, and of what the rest of his life was like once it had.

fields.title: Introduction: The Life He Told, and the Life the Letters Tell
fields.body_html:
“Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts.”

— Proverbs 21:2, KJV

C. S. Lewis disliked writing about himself. He disliked being asked about himself, and he was suspicious of the modern habit of reading an author’s books as clues to his private life. He thought that a poem or a story should be looked at, not through. It is an irony he would have enjoyed, or perhaps resented, that he has become one of the most written-about Christians of the twentieth century. There are dozens of biographies, several films, plays and novels, a stream of scholarly studies, and an industry of quotations, some genuine and many not. Anyone who tries to tell his life now has to make his way through a great deal of material, and through a few well-worn legends.

His Own Account

Lewis did tell part of his story himself. Surprised by Joy, published in 1955 when he was fifty-six, is the account of his childhood, his schooling, his loss of faith and his long road back to it. It is a brilliant book, funny and sharp and searching, and it remains the indispensable source for his early life. But it is not a full autobiography, and it never claims to be. Lewis said plainly that he was telling the story of his conversion, and only those parts of his life that bore upon it. The book stops in 1931, more than thirty years before his death. It says very little about the war, almost nothing about the Moore household in which he lived for three decades, and nothing at all about his marriage, which had not yet happened.

It also has the weaknesses of all memory. Lewis wrote it in his fifties about events in his childhood and youth, and he wrote it with a purpose. Some of his judgements were sharpened by hindsight. His picture of his father is affectionate but also, many readers have felt, unfair. His account of his English schools is so bitter that his brother, who had attended one of them and liked it, thought it badly overdrawn. And at least one of his dates, the year he came to believe in God, appears to be wrong, as we shall see.

The Letters and the Diaries

Fortunately Lewis was one of the great letter-writers of his age, and an enormous number of his letters survive. They have been gathered and edited by Walter Hooper, a young American who became his secretary for a few weeks in 1963 and spent the rest of his long life serving his literary legacy. The Collected Letters fill three thick volumes, and they let us follow Lewis almost week by week from his schooldays to the end. His letters to his boyhood friend Arthur Greeves, written over nearly fifty years, are especially revealing, because Greeves was the one person to whom he told almost everything.

His brother Warren kept a diary for most of his adult life. A selection was published in 1982 under the title Brothers and Friends, and Warren also wrote a short memoir of his brother which was printed with the first collection of Lewis’s letters in 1966. Warren’s testimony is precious, because he knew Jack better and longer than anyone. But it has its own colouring. He loved his brother fiercely, he disliked Mrs Moore intensely, and in his later years he wrote some things in bitterness that he might have softened in health.

There are also the memories of friends, pupils and colleagues, recorded in books and interviews over many decades, and the published letters and diaries of others in his circle, especially Tolkien. And there are the records kept by colleges, regiments, hospitals and registry offices, which can sometimes settle a question that memory leaves open.

The Biographers

The first full biography was written by two of his friends, Roger Lancelyn Green and Walter Hooper, and published in 1974. It is warm, detailed and close to its subject. George Sayer, a former pupil who became a close friend, published Jack in 1988, a book many readers still think the best portrait of the man. A. N. Wilson’s biography of 1990 was livelier and more sceptical, and it provoked argument for some of its claims. Alan Jacobs wrote a fine study of Lewis’s imagination, The Narnian, in 2005. In 2013, the fiftieth anniversary of Lewis’s death, Alister McGrath published a biography that went back to the letters and re-examined the chronology, and it changed some long-accepted dates. Philip and Carol Zaleski’s The Fellowship of 2015 set Lewis among the other Inklings. Abigail Santamaria’s life of Joy Davidman, also of 2015, told the marriage from Joy’s side. This book has drawn on all of them, and its debts are listed in the last appendix.

Where the Sources Disagree

On most of the facts of Lewis’s life the sources agree. On a few they do not, and it is better to name them at the start.

The first is the date of his conversion to belief in God. Lewis placed it in the summer term of 1929. McGrath, reading the letters closely, has argued that it must have been the summer of 1930, and most scholars now accept his case, though not all. This book gives both dates and explains the reasoning in its place.

The second is the nature of Lewis’s relationship with Janie Moore, the mother of his dead friend, with whom he lived from 1919 until her death in 1951. Some biographers believe that in its early years it was a love affair. Others believe it was always the relationship of a young man to a woman who had become a second mother to him. Lewis never explained it, and the evidence is incomplete. This book sets out what is known and what is guessed, and does not pretend to settle what cannot be settled.

The third is a cluster of smaller matters: the exact date of the famous ride to Whipsnade Zoo, the story of his supposed humiliation at the hands of the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe, and several details of his marriage that later films and plays have rearranged for dramatic effect. Each is dealt with where it falls.

The Legends

Some stories about Lewis are simply false, and it does no honour to him to repeat them. He did not lose his faith in reason after a debate in 1948. He did not abandon his Christian writing in old age. The film Shadowlands, which many people know better than any book, changed the ages of Joy’s sons, left one of them out entirely, and invented scenes and words that never happened, as films do. And a great many sayings attributed to Lewis on the internet are not his at all. This book quotes him only three times, each time from a published book and with the source given. Everything else is told in its own words.

What Kind of Book This Is

This is a Christian biography. It does not pretend to be neutral about the faith Lewis came to hold, but it does try to be fair to the man, including his faults. Lewis had no patience with a cult of personality, and he disliked fuss about himself above almost anything. The truth about a sinner whom God was mending is more use to other sinners than a legend about a saint, and it gives the glory where it belongs. He would want his life told straight. That is what the following chapters attempt.

fields.title: Little Lea
fields.body_html:
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”

— Proverbs 22:6, KJV

A Belfast Family

Clive Staples Lewis was born on 29 November 1898 in a semi-detached house called Dundela Villas, in Strandtown, on the eastern edge of Belfast. Belfast at the end of the nineteenth century was a city of shipyards, linen mills and rope works, proud, industrious and deeply Protestant. From the hills above Strandtown one could see the great gantries of the Harland and Wolff yard, where a few years later the Titanic would be built. Lewis grew up within sight of the cranes and within sound of the ships’ sirens on the lough, and for the rest of his life he loved the soft, wet Ulster countryside of hills, mists and distant sea.

His father, Albert James Lewis, was a solicitor with a practice in the police courts. Albert was the son of a Welsh boilermaker who had settled in Ireland and done well in the shipbuilding trade. He was clever, emotional, fond of oratory and of long words, a keen reader and an anxious man. He loved his sons deeply and never found an easy way to show it. His wife, Florence Augusta Hamilton, always called Flora, came from a different world. Her father, the Reverend Thomas Hamilton, was rector of St Mark’s, Dundela, the parish church where the Lewis boys were baptised. Flora was quiet, humorous and unusually well educated. She had studied at Queen’s College in Belfast and had taken a degree with honours in logic and mathematics, at a time when very few women anywhere went to university at all. Albert courted her for years before she agreed to marry him in 1894.

fields.title: August 1908
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.”

— Psalm 27:10, KJV

The Illness

Early in 1908 Flora Lewis fell ill. The doctors found cancer. In those days an operation for cancer was often performed at home, and Flora’s was carried out at Little Lea, with the household doing its best to go on around it. For a while she seemed to rally. She was taken to the seaside to recover, and Jack went with her. Then, in the summer, the disease returned. The house filled with nurses, doctors and the smell of antiseptic. Normal life stopped. The boys were kept out of the sickroom and did not understand what was happening, except that everything had changed.

It was a terrible year for Albert. His own father died in the spring of 1908. His wife was dying through the summer. Within weeks of her death his brother Joseph died too. Albert was a man of strong feeling and little self-command, and under the weight of these losses he became, for a time, almost a stranger to his sons: given to outbursts of grief and temper, absorbed in his own suffering, unable to reach the two frightened boys who were watching him.

A Prayer That Seemed to Fail

Jack prayed. He had been taught that God answers prayer, and he believed it, in the way a nine-year-old believes. He prayed that his mother would be made well. When she died, on 23 August 1908, he prayed that she would be restored to life. Nothing happened.

Looking back nearly fifty years later, Lewis did not describe this as the moment he lost his faith. He was careful about it. He thought that the prayer had not really been addressed to the God of the Christians at all. He had approached God, he said, not as a Saviour or a Judge but as a kind of magician who would do what was asked and then go away. When the magic did not work, he was not shattered; he was simply left with nothing. But he came to believe that the episode laid a foundation for the unbelief that followed. A child who has asked God for something with all his heart and been refused learns something, even if he does not yet know what he has learned.

Flora was forty-six. On the day she died, the leaf on the Shakespeare calendar in her bedroom carried a line from King Lear: “Men must endure their going hence.” Albert kept the leaf. More than half a century later, Warren had those words cut on his brother’s gravestone.

The End of a World

Lewis wrote, looking back, that his mother’s death took from him every certainty and every settled happiness he had known. It is the kind of judgement that can sound like the exaggeration of a memoir, but it is borne out by everything that happened next. The two boys, he said, drew closer together and further from their father. From then on they had, in effect, only each other. They loved Albert and pitied him, but they no longer trusted him to understand them, and they began to keep their real lives from him. It was the beginning of a habit of concealment that would last for twenty years.

There is a tender detail from those weeks. Lewis remembered being taken into the room where his mother lay dead, and being horrified by what he saw: not the face he had known but something strange. He also remembered hating the paraphernalia of the funeral: the flowers, the hearse, the black clothes. He was a sensitive child, and the outward show of death seemed to him an assault. Long afterwards, when he came to write about grief, he wrote with the knowledge of someone who had first met it at nine years old and had never quite recovered from the meeting.

Sent Away

Less than a month after Flora’s death, Albert did what many fathers of his class would have done. He sent both boys to boarding school in England. Warnie had already been at Wynyard School in Watford, Hertfordshire, for three years. Now Jack went with him. They crossed the Irish Sea by the night boat from Belfast to Fleetwood, and took the train south. It was the first of many such crossings, and Lewis never forgot the misery of them: the smell of the boat, the dark, grey dawn over Lancashire, and the knowledge that he was being carried away from everything he knew.

Wynyard was a small private school run by a clergyman named Robert Capron, whom the boys called Oldie. It was, by every account including Warnie’s, a bad school. Capron was a brutal and erratic man who beat the boys for little or no reason and taught them almost nothing. The school was dwindling, and within two years it would close. Capron was afterwards certified insane. In Surprised by Joy Lewis gave Wynyard a bitter nickname taken from the Nazi camps, which he regretted, and which shows how deeply the place had hurt him. The detail most worth remembering is a different one. At Wynyard, for the first time, Jack was taken regularly to a High Church parish where he heard the Christian faith taught as if it mattered. He began to pray seriously and to read his Bible. For a short time, in that unhappy place, he was something like a believing boy.

What the Psalm Promises

The verse at the head of this chapter is from Psalm 27. Its words are almost too apt. Jack’s mother had been taken, and his father, in grief, had withdrawn and sent him away. Neither parent had meant to forsake him, but in every sense a child can feel, he was forsaken. The psalmist does not say that this will not happen. He says what God does when it does: “then the LORD will take me up.”

For many years nothing in Lewis’s life looked like the fulfilment of that promise. He lost what little faith he had and went on to deny that there was any God to take him up. But the psalm does not set a timetable. Thirty years later, a middle-aged man who had once prayed for his mother’s life would write to bereaved strangers with a tenderness that came from his own wound. The child who was carried across the sea in the dark had been taken up after all. He simply did not know it yet.

fields.title: Schools, and a Faith Let Go
fields.body_html:
“The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.”

— Psalm 14:1, KJV

Campbell and Cherbourg

Wynyard closed in the summer of 1910 for want of pupils, and for one term that autumn Jack went to Campbell College in Belfast, a mile or so from home. He liked being near Little Lea, but he was ill with a chest complaint and Albert took him away before Christmas. In January 1911 he was sent back to England, to a preparatory school called Cherbourg House in the spa town of Malvern, in Worcestershire. Warnie was by then a pupil at Malvern College, the public school on the hill above it, so the brothers were again within reach of each other.

Cherbourg was a far better school than Wynyard, and Jack spent two and a half years there. He worked hard, read widely and in 1913 won a classical scholarship to Malvern College. But it was at Cherbourg, between the ages of twelve and fourteen, that he quietly ceased to be a Christian. He gave several reasons for it, looking back, and none of them was dramatic.

How the Faith Went

One reason was a kind and sympathetic matron, whom Lewis later wrote of with real affection. She had drifted away from conventional Christianity into a vague world of spiritualism and theosophy, and she talked about it to the boys. She did not set out to unsettle anyone. But to a clever, lonely boy, her talk had the effect of loosening the outlines of the faith he had been taught. If there were many paths and many mysteries, the plain creed of St Mark’s, Dundela, seemed less solid than before.

A second reason was the way he had been trying to pray. At Wynyard he had become anxious about his prayers. He thought that a prayer did not count unless he felt the right things while saying it, and he would lie awake night after night, saying his prayers over and over, trying to produce the proper feelings and never succeeding. It became a torment. Lewis later thought that this false and scrupulous religion, which put the weight on his own inner state rather than on God, made the faith a burden he was glad to put down. When he did put it down, the relief was enormous.

A third reason went deeper. Even as a boy he was struck by the waste, cruelty and indifference of the universe. He read the ancient poets and noticed that their gods were treated as fables by every modern scholar, and he could see no reason why the God of the Christians should be treated differently. Why should Christianity alone be true, out of all the religions of the world? No one he knew could give him an answer that satisfied him, and he did not much want one.

So, without fuss and without telling anyone, he stopped believing. There was no crisis. There was simply the end of something that had never been very strong. He went on saying his prayers in public and going to chapel, because that was expected. Inwardly, he was finished with it.

Malvern College

In September 1913 Jack followed Warnie to Malvern College. Warnie had loved the place. Jack hated it from the first week. Malvern, like most English public schools of the time, was ruled by the senior boys, the athletes and prefects who were called the Bloods. Junior boys were their servants. They cleaned shoes, carried messages and ran errands at all hours. The school worshipped games, at which Jack was useless. He also hated what he saw of its moral life: the snobbery, the social climbing, and a pervasive culture of sexual favouritism among the boys, which he wrote about frankly forty years later.

Lewis’s account of Malvern in Surprised by Joy is very bitter, and Warnie, reading it, thought it unjust. The truth probably lies between them. Jack was a shy, clever, bookish boy who did not fit, and he was miserable. He was exhausted by the fagging, he slept badly, and he developed a lasting contempt for the whole system of popularity and power. Lewis’s later preoccupation with pride, with the desire to belong to an inner ring, and with the misery of trying to keep up with the right people, all have roots in that year. He would write and preach about such things as a grown man, and those who heard him knew that he was speaking from experience.

There were consolations. Malvern had a good library, and a master named Harry Wakelyn Smith, whom the boys called Smewgy, who taught the classics with a love of poetry that Jack never forgot. And in his reading he discovered the northern myths. A few years before, he had come upon a picture and a few lines about the death of the Norse god Balder, and the old longing had flooded back. Now he read everything he could find about the gods of the north: the sagas, Wagner’s operas in summary, the stories of Asgard and Valhalla. He found in them a beauty he did not find in the religion of his childhood.

Arthur Greeves

During the Easter holidays of 1914, at Little Lea, Jack met a boy from the house across the road who was ill in bed. His name was Arthur Greeves. He was three years older than Jack, the son of a well-to-do Belfast family of Plymouth Brethren background, gentle, artistic and often in poor health. Jack had known him slightly and never thought much of him. Then he saw a book on Arthur’s bed. It was a book of Norse mythology. Arthur asked whether Jack liked it. Jack said that he did. And in a moment, as Lewis remembered it, each discovered that the other loved exactly the same things.

It was the beginning of a friendship that lasted until Lewis died. For nearly fifty years the two wrote to each other, and Lewis told Arthur things that he told no one else: his doubts, his reading, his temptations, and, years later, the stages of his conversion. Arthur was a Christian, though for some years an uncertain one, and Jack teased him for it. He could not have guessed that the letters he was writing would one day be read by scholars as the most intimate record of his long road back to God.

What the Psalm Says

The verse at the head of this chapter is blunt. In the language of the Psalms the fool is not a person of low intelligence but one who lives as though God were not there. By any worldly measure Jack Lewis was not a fool. He was one of the cleverest boys in the British Isles. But at fourteen he had decided in his heart that there was no God, and he would spend the next sixteen years living by that decision. Lewis himself would later have agreed with the psalm’s verdict. He thought that unbelief was rarely a matter of reasoning alone. It was a matter of the heart, and his own heart, at Cherbourg and Malvern, had wanted very much to be left alone.

He also hated what he saw of its moral life: the snobbery, the social climbing, and a pervasive culture of sexual favouritism among the boys, which he wrote about frankly forty years later. Lewis’s account of Malvern in Surprised by Joy is very bitter, and Warnie, reading it, thought it unjust. The truth probably lies between them. Jack was a shy, clever, bookish boy who did not fit, and he was miserable. He was exhausted by the fagging, he slept badly, and he developed a lasting contempt for the whole system of popularity and power. Lewis’s later preoccupation with pride, with the desire to belong to an inner ring, and with the misery of trying to keep up with the right people, all have roots in that year. He would write and preach about such things as a grown man, and those who heard him knew that he was speaking from experience. There were consolations. Malvern had a good library, and a master named Harry Wakelyn Smith, whom the boys called Smewgy, who taught the classics with a love of poetry that Jack never forgot. And in his reading he discovered the northern myths. A few years before, he had come upon a picture and a few lines about the death of the Norse god Balder, and the old longing had flooded back. Now he read everything he could find about the gods of the north: the sagas, Wagner’s operas in summary, the stories of Asgard and Valhalla. He found in them a beauty he did not find in the religion of his childhood. Arthur Greeves During the Easter holidays of 1914, at Little Lea, Jack met a boy from the house across the road who was ill in bed. His name was Arthur Greeves. He was three years older than Jack, the son of a well-to-do Belfast family of Plymouth Brethren background, gentle, artistic and often in poor health. Jack had known him slightly and never thought much of him. Then he saw a book on Arthur’s bed. It was a book of Norse mythology. Arthur asked whether Jack liked it. Jack said that he did. And in a moment, as Lewis remembered it, each discovered that the other loved exactly the same things. It was the beginning of a friendship that lasted until Lewis died. For nearly fifty years the two wrote to each other, and Lewis told Arthur things that he told no one else: his doubts, his reading, his temptations, and, years later, the stages of his conversion. Arthur was a Christian, though for some years an uncertain one, and Jack teased him for it. He could not have guessed that the letters he was writing would one day be read by scholars as the most intimate record of his long road back to God. What the Psalm Says The verse at the head of this chapter is blunt. In the language of the Psalms the fool is not a person of low intelligence but one who lives as though God were not there. By any worldly measure Jack Lewis was not a fool. He was one of the cleverest boys in the British Isles. But at fourteen he had decided in his heart that there was no God, and he would spend the next sixteen years living by that decision. Lewis himself would later have agreed with the psalm’s verdict. He thought that unbelief was rarely a matter of reasoning alone. It was a matter of the heart, and his own heart, at Cherbourg and Malvern, had wanted very much to be left alone.

fields.body_html:
“Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.”

— Proverbs 27:17, KJV

A Way Out

Jack’s letters home from Malvern were so wretched that even Albert, who often misread his sons, could see that something had to be done. Warnie, who was by then preparing for the Royal Military College at Sandhurst, had been sent to a private tutor, and had done well. In the summer of 1914 Albert decided to send Jack to the same man. In September of that year, a month after the outbreak of the Great War, the fifteen-year-old arrived at a house called Gastons in the village of Great Bookham, in Surrey, to be prepared for university by William Thompson Kirkpatrick.

Kirkpatrick had been Albert’s own headmaster at Lurgan College in County Armagh years before. He was by now retired, living with his wife in the Surrey countryside and taking a few private pupils. Albert called him the Great Knock, and so did his sons. He was a tall, lean, ruthless Ulster Scot with side whiskers and a voice like a bell, who had been brought up a Presbyterian and become a convinced atheist. He did not talk about religion much. He simply assumed that no intelligent man could believe it.

The Lesson on the Platform

Lewis told a story of his first meeting with Kirkpatrick that became famous. As they walked from the railway station, Jack, trying to make polite conversation, remarked that the Surrey countryside was wilder than he had expected. Kirkpatrick stopped and asked him what he meant by wild, and what grounds he had for expecting anything else. Within a few minutes the boy had been shown that he had no clear idea of what he had said, no evidence for his expectation, and therefore no right to an opinion at all. Kirkpatrick did not mean it unkindly. It was simply how he spoke. Every remark, however casual, was treated as a proposition to be defended.

Many boys would have been crushed. Jack loved it. For the first time in his life he was being taken seriously by a grown man. He learned to define his terms, to look for evidence, to spot a bad argument at a hundred yards and to say exactly what he meant. He would later say that he owed Kirkpatrick more than he owed almost any other teacher, and the debt is visible on nearly every page he wrote. The clarity of his prose, his habit of beginning with a definition, his relish for an argument and his impatience with muddle were learned in that house in Surrey.

Homer in Surrey

Kirkpatrick’s method of teaching languages was as direct as his conversation. On Jack’s first morning he sat down with him, opened Homer in Greek, read a passage aloud and translated it, and then left the boy to go on alone with a lexicon. Jack was soon reading Homer at speed and thinking in Greek. He read Latin the same way, and before he left Bookham he had added French, Italian and some German. The two and a half years were among the happiest of his life. He worked in the mornings, walked the Surrey lanes in the afternoons, read for himself in the evenings, and wrote long letters to Arthur Greeves about everything he read.

He also settled into his unbelief. Kirkpatrick never preached atheism to him, but the whole atmosphere of the house was rationalist, and Jack absorbed it. By sixteen he was writing to Arthur, with all the confidence of youth, that all religions were mythologies invented by human beings, that Christianity was one among them, and that he believed in none. He thought of himself as a hard-headed realist, and in his mind the beauty he loved in poetry and myth and the bleak universe described by science were two separate worlds that had nothing to do with each other.

A Confirmation He Regretted

There is one sad episode from these years. In December 1914, during the Christmas holidays, Jack was confirmed at St Mark’s, Dundela, and took his first Communion. He did it to please his father, and because he could not face the argument that would follow if he refused. He did not believe a word of it. Years later he looked back on this as one of the worst things he had ever done. He had, as he saw it, made a solemn act before God in a spirit of complete unbelief, and he had done it out of cowardice. It is a measure of how seriously the older Lewis took the sacraments that he never forgave himself lightly for that day.

A Book Bought at a Station

In March 1916 Jack was waiting at Leatherhead station for a train. He picked a cheap copy of a book off the station bookstall and bought it to read on the journey. It was Phantastes, a romance first published in 1858 by George MacDonald, a Scottish Congregational minister who had been forced out of his pulpit and had made his living as a writer and lecturer. The story follows a young man through a dreamlike fairy country of forests, castles and shadows.

Lewis read it that night and was overwhelmed. He wrote to Arthur that he had had a great literary experience. What he found in it he could not name for many years. It was not that the book persuaded him of anything. He had no idea, then, that MacDonald was a Christian, or that the quality that moved him so deeply had anything to do with the Christian faith. But he felt that a new kind of goodness had touched the longing he had known since childhood. The longing itself seemed cleaner and brighter afterwards, as if it had been washed. The verdict he gave in Surprised by Joy is one of the best-known sentences he ever wrote about himself: that the book had begun to work on his imagination, and that the rest of him took much longer to follow.

He was right about the delay. It would be fifteen years before the rest of him caught up. But George MacDonald became, in time, the writer Lewis loved and honoured above all others. Late in life he edited an anthology of MacDonald’s writings and called him his master. When, in one of his own stories, Lewis came to put a wise guide into a strange country, the guide was George MacDonald.

Iron Sharpening Iron

The verse at the head of this chapter speaks of friends sharpening each other, as one iron blade sharpens another. It describes the Bookham years well. An old atheist sharpened a young one, and the edge he put on Jack Lewis’s mind would one day be turned against everything Kirkpatrick believed. Kirkpatrick died in 1921, long before his pupil became a Christian, and we do not know what he would have made of it. But a God who uses unbelievers to prepare his servants is not hard to find in Scripture. Cyrus of Persia was called God’s shepherd without ever knowing God’s name. In a Surrey village, a ruthless logician who thought religion nonsense was training the most effective Christian apologist of his century.

fields.title: A Promise at Keble
fields.body_html:
“When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.”

— Ecclesiastes 5:4, KJV

Oxford at War

In December 1916 Jack sat the scholarship examinations at Oxford and was elected to a classical scholarship at University College, one of the oldest colleges in the university. There was a difficulty. To matriculate, every Oxford man had to pass an entrance examination called Responsions, which included elementary mathematics, and Jack, who could translate Homer at sight, could not do sums. He failed the mathematics paper in March 1917. He would almost certainly have failed it again. In the end the war solved the problem for him: after the armistice, men who had served were excused the examination.

He came up to University College in April 1917, but there was not much of a university to come up to. The war had emptied Oxford. Most of the young men were in France, the colleges were half given over to hospitals and military training, and the halls where Jack had expected to hear lectures were full of convalescent soldiers. He had only one term as an undergraduate before the army took him. As an Irishman he was exempt from conscription, which never applied in Ireland. He chose to serve anyway. He joined the university’s Officers’ Training Corps, and in June 1917 he was posted to a cadet battalion that was quartered in Keble College, a few minutes’ walk away.

Paddy Moore

The cadets at Keble were billeted two to a room. Jack’s room-mate was Edward Francis Courtenay Moore, always called Paddy. He was almost exactly Jack’s age, and like him he was Irish. He had been born in Dublin and had grown up partly in Bristol, where his mother had moved after separating from her husband. His mother, Janie King Moore, had come to Oxford to be near him during his training, bringing with her Paddy’s eleven-year-old sister Maureen.

Jack and Paddy became friends, and Jack was soon spending his free time with the Moores. Mrs Moore was forty-five, warm, talkative, generous, and in the habit of mothering every young man her son brought home. She had been unhappily married to a Dublin civil engineer whom she called, in letters, the Beast, and she lived on a small allowance from him. She had none of Flora Lewis’s learning. But she had a household, and a kitchen table, and a welcome. To a motherless young man of eighteen, who had been sent away from home at nine and had spent the years since among schoolmasters, it was a great deal.

The Promise

It was at some point in these months that Jack and Paddy made a promise to each other. If one of them was killed in France and the other survived, the survivor would look after the dead man’s parent. We know of the promise from Maureen, who remembered it many years later, and from the way Lewis behaved afterwards, which makes sense only if such a promise was made. It was the kind of pact that many young officers made in that war, half in solemnity and half to keep up their courage. Few of them can have kept it as Jack Lewis did.

A Silence Kept From Albert

Jack’s letters to his father during these months mention the Moores only in passing. His letters to Arthur Greeves say much more, and they hint at feelings he would not put down in plain words. He spent most of his leave before embarkation not in Belfast, as Albert expected, but with the Moores in Bristol. Albert was hurt and puzzled. It was the beginning of a concealment that would grow over the next ten years until it became one of the burdens of Jack’s conscience. The young man who had learned at nine to keep his real life from his father was now hiding from him the most important relationship he had.

Commission and Embarkation

In September 1917 Jack was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the 3rd Battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry. Paddy was commissioned in the Rifle Brigade. They parted in the autumn of that year. Jack was given leave and then ordered to the front. He crossed to France in mid-November and reached the trenches on 29 November 1917, his nineteenth birthday.

Paddy went to France too. In March 1918 the German army launched its great spring offensive, the last throw of the war, and the British line was driven back across the old battlefields of the Somme. Paddy Moore was posted missing in the fighting in late March. Some months later his family was told that he had been killed near Péronne. He was nineteen.

The Vow

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the Preacher, who had seen many vows made and few kept. He warns that a vow should not be made lightly, and that once it is made it should be paid without delay. The promise at Keble was not made to God. Neither young man then believed in God. But it was a promise, solemnly given, and Jack Lewis paid it in full. He paid it for more than thirty years, through poverty and plenty, through his conversion and his fame, at the cost of much of his freedom and of a good deal of his peace. Whatever else may be said of the household that grew out of that promise, it should first be said that a young unbeliever kept his word.

fields.title: 15 April 1918
fields.body_html:
“A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee.”

— Psalm 91:7, KJV

The Trenches

Lewis said very little about the war, then or later. In Surprised by Joy he gave it only a few pages, and he said frankly that he had put most of it out of his mind. He mentioned in a few lines the cold, the mud, the weariness, the wounded and the unburied dead. He mentioned that the war was in a curious way unreal to him, as if it were happening to someone else. He was not a professional soldier, and he never pretended to have been a brave one. He did his duty, he endured, and when it was over he tried, with only partial success, to forget it.

His battalion held a sector of the line near Arras, in northern France. The winter of 1917 to 1918 was hard, and in February he fell ill with trench fever, a disease carried by lice that brought high temperatures and aching bones. He spent three weeks in a hospital at Le Tréport on the Channel coast. His letters home from there are almost cheerful: he had a bed, clean sheets and books. He read and recovered and in March went back to his battalion, just as the great German offensive broke.

The Shell

The Somerset Light Infantry were not at the centre of the March onslaught, but in April the Germans attacked again further north, on the River Lys, and Jack’s battalion was thrown into the fighting near the village of Mont-Bernenchon. On 14 April the battalion attacked. During the confused fighting Lewis was credited with taking the surrender of some sixty German soldiers, who appeared out of the smoke with their hands up and gave themselves up to him. He was always modest about it. As he told it, taking them amounted to discovering, with great relief, that they wished to surrender.

The next day, 15 April 1918, a shell burst close beside him. It was almost certainly a British shell falling short. Lewis was hit in three places: in the left hand, in the leg, and in the chest, where a fragment lodged below his armpit. The sergeant who was standing next to him, Harry Ayres, was killed outright. Lewis remembered Ayres afterwards with gratitude and affection. He had been a kind, steady man who had looked after his young and inexperienced officer, and Lewis felt that he owed him a great deal.

Lewis was carried back through the casualty stations to a base hospital at Étaples. His wounds were serious but not fatal. Some of the metal was removed at once. A fragment in his chest was left where it was, and he carried it for more than twenty-five years before it was finally taken out in 1944.

The Hospital in London

In late May he was brought back to England and admitted to a hospital in London. He wrote to his father, asking him to come. Albert, who was nervous of travel, set in his routines, and perhaps unable to face it, did not come. Jack wrote again. Albert still did not come. Through the whole of that summer and autumn, while his son lay wounded and then convalescent in England, Albert Lewis never once crossed the Irish Sea to see him.

It is easy to judge Albert harshly for this, and Jack did judge him harshly. But Albert was a widower of fifty-four, frightened of change, who had never been a traveller. His elder son was also at the front, and he was sick with anxiety for both of them. None of that made his absence hurt any less. Jack never forgot it.

Someone else did come. Janie Moore, who had by then been told that her own son was missing, came at once. She visited Jack in hospital, wrote to him and fussed over him, and when he was transferred in June to a convalescent hospital he asked to be sent to one near Bristol, where the Moores lived. He was moved to other camps and hospitals later in the year, and she followed. By the time news came that Paddy had certainly been killed, the bond between the wounded young officer and the bereaved mother was already strong. Jack had kept his promise before he knew he would have to.

A Book of Poems

While he was convalescing, Lewis prepared a collection of the poems he had written since his schooldays. It was published in March 1919 under the name Clive Hamilton, taking his mother’s maiden name, with the title Spirits in Bondage. The poems are those of a young man who has seen the war and believes that the universe is either empty or ruled by a cruel power. They are angry, sad and sometimes beautiful, and they set out a creed of defiant atheism. A few readers noticed them. Most did not. Lewis was disappointed but not discouraged. For the next decade his chief ambition was to be a poet.

The Survivor

In December 1918, a month after the armistice, Lewis was demobilised. He went home to Belfast for Christmas, and his father and brother met him with enormous relief. Then, in January 1919, he went back to Oxford to resume his degree. He was twenty years old. He had been a soldier for eighteen months, and he had been wounded, and his closest friend from training was dead. Many of the young men who had trained with him at Keble had been killed.

Lewis did not talk about survivor’s guilt, and he would not have liked the phrase. But he knew that he had been spared when others were not, and he knew that he had no explanation for it. The verse at the head of this chapter is from the ninety-first psalm, which many soldiers carried into that war and many did not carry out. It is not a promise that no believer will ever be hurt, for believers fell in their thousands on the Somme. It is a confession that every life is in the hand of God, and that those who are spared are spared for a purpose. Lewis did not yet believe in that hand. But it had been over him on 15 April 1918, and in time he would come to see it.

On 14 April the battalion attacked. During the confused fighting Lewis was credited with taking the surrender of some sixty German soldiers, who appeared out of the smoke with their hands up and gave themselves up to him. He was always modest about it. As he told it, taking them amounted to discovering, with great relief, that they wished to surrender. The next day, 15 April 1918, a shell burst close beside him. It was almost certainly a British shell falling short. Lewis was hit in three places: in the left hand, in the leg, and in the chest, where a fragment lodged below his armpit. The sergeant who was standing next to him, Harry Ayres, was killed outright. Lewis remembered Ayres afterwards with gratitude and affection. He had been a kind, steady man who had looked after his young and inexperienced officer, and Lewis felt that he owed him a great deal. Lewis was carried back through the casualty stations to a base hospital at Étaples. His wounds were serious but not fatal. Some of the metal was removed at once. A fragment in his chest was left where it was, and he carried it for more than twenty-five years before it was finally taken out in 1944. The Hospital in London In late May he was brought back to England and admitted to a hospital in London. He wrote to his father, asking him to come. Albert, who was nervous of travel, set in his routines, and perhaps unable to face it, did not come. Jack wrote again. Albert still did not come. Through the whole of that summer and autumn, while his son lay wounded and then convalescent in England, Albert Lewis never once crossed the Irish Sea to see him. It is easy to judge Albert harshly for this, and Jack did judge him harshly. But Albert was a widower of fifty-four, frightened of change, who had never been a traveller. His elder son was also at the front, and he was sick with anxiety for both of them. None of that made his absence hurt any less. Jack never forgot it. Someone else did come. She visited Jack in hospital, wrote to him and fussed over him, and when he was transferred in June to a convalescent hospital he asked to be sent to one near Bristol, where the Moores lived. He was moved to other camps and hospitals later in the year, and she followed. He went home to Belfast for Christmas, and his father and brother met him with enormous relief. Then, in January 1919, he went back to Oxford to resume his degree. He was twenty years old. He had been a soldier for eighteen months, and he had been wounded, and his closest friend from training was dead. Many of the young men who had trained with him at Keble had been killed. Lewis did not talk about survivor’s guilt, and he would not have liked the phrase. But he knew that he had been spared when others were not, and he knew that he had no explanation for it. The verse at the head of this chapter is from the ninety-first psalm, which many soldiers carried into that war and many did not carry out. It is not a promise that no believer will ever be hurt, for believers fell in their thousands on the Somme. It is a confession that every life is in the hand of God, and that those who are spared are spared for a purpose. Lewis did not yet believe in that hand. But it had been over him on 15 April 1918, and in time he would come to see it.

fields.body_html:
“Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.”

— James 1:27, KJV

A Household in Oxford

When Lewis returned to Oxford in January 1919, Janie Moore and Maureen came too. Mrs Moore took rooms in the city, and within a short time Jack was spending most of his time outside college hours with them. Undergraduates were required to live in college, so for a while he kept up the appearance of a normal student life while in fact dividing his days between University College and the Moores’ lodgings. As soon as the rules allowed, he moved in with them. For the next thirty years, apart from his college rooms, he had no other home.

It was a precarious household. Mrs Moore had very little money: an irregular allowance from her estranged husband and nothing else. Jack had his scholarship and an allowance from his father, which Albert paid on the understanding that his son was living as a student. The two incomes together barely kept them. In the first years they moved again and again from one set of rented rooms to another, often to cheaper and colder lodgings, with Mrs Moore taking in lodgers to make ends meet. In 1922 they settled in a rented house called Hillsboro on the Western Road in Headington, on the eastern edge of Oxford, and stayed there for eight years.

Lewis did the shopping, washed up, ran errands, tutored Maureen in Latin, walked the dog, and studied when he could find a quiet hour. His diary from these years, which he kept from 1922 to 1927 and which was later published, is full of the minor crises of domestic life: a sick maid, a smoking chimney, a quarrel with a lodger, Mrs Moore’s headaches, money worries. It is also full of reading, walking, conversation and hard work. It is the diary of a man who was very busy, often tired, and not unhappy.

What Albert Was Not Told

Albert was told almost nothing. He knew that his son had a friendship with the mother of a dead comrade, and he did not like what little he knew. But he did not know that Jack was living with Mrs Moore, and he did not know that the allowance he was sending was partly keeping her household. Jack deceived him, sometimes by silence and sometimes by direct lies, and he went on doing so for ten years. Warnie, who was serving abroad, knew more and disapproved.

Lewis came to regard this deception as one of the great sins of his life. He had taken his father’s money under false pretences, he had kept from him the central fact of his life, and he had done it partly out of fear and partly out of contempt. When, after his conversion, he looked back over the years of his unbelief, it was not his intellectual errors that troubled him most. It was this.

What Was the Relationship?

This is the place to ask a question that every biographer has had to ask and none has been able to answer with certainty. What exactly was the relationship between Jack Lewis and Janie Moore?

She was twenty-six years older than he was. She was still legally married. She became, in his letters and in the life of the household, something between a mother, a landlady and a companion. He called her Minto, after a brand of sweets, and in letters to others he often called her his mother. Many people who met them in the 1920s and 1930s assumed that she was his mother, and he did not correct them.

Some biographers believe that in the first years, at least, the two were lovers. They point to the intensity of Jack’s feelings for her in 1917 and 1918, to the secrecy with which he surrounded the relationship, to hints in his letters to Arthur Greeves, and to the fact that a young man of twenty and a lonely woman of forty-six were living together under circumstances that would have suggested an affair to anyone in that age. A. N. Wilson and Alister McGrath both think it likely. George Sayer, who knew Lewis well, came to think it probable too, though he had once doubted it.

Others are certain that it was never anything but a filial relationship. They point out that the household always included Maureen, a child and then a young woman living at home. They note that Lewis never spoke of it in such terms to anyone, and that Warnie, who disliked Mrs Moore intensely and had every reason to suspect the worst, came to see her chiefly as a tyrant in the house, not as Jack’s mistress. Walter Hooper always insisted that the relationship was one of a son to an adopted mother.

The honest answer is that we do not know. There is no letter or record that settles it, and Lewis, who was otherwise remarkably open about his own sins, kept this part of his life closed. If the relationship began as a love affair, it seems clear that it did not remain one, and certainly not after his conversion. What is beyond dispute is what came after. For more than thirty years Lewis supported Mrs Moore, lived with her, served her and nursed her, through her decline into a querulous, demanding and often difficult old age, until her death in 1951. Whatever the relationship was at the beginning, at the end it was a long, costly act of faithfulness.

Not an Easy House

Some of Lewis’s friends found the household baffling and some found it painful. Mrs Moore was generous, hospitable and kind in many ways. She fed half the stray animals of Headington, she was devoted to Maureen, and she worked hard. But she was also possessive, anxious and a constant source of small demands. She liked to have Jack at her beck and call. She would interrupt his work for errands that could have waited, and she seems to have had little interest in his books or his ideas. Friends who came to the house noticed how often Jack was called away from conversation to some domestic task, and some of them resented it on his behalf.

Lewis almost never complained. In his letters he spoke of her with loyalty, sometimes with humour, and later, as she grew old and ill, with patience. He seems to have regarded the burdens of that house as part of what he owed: to Paddy, to her, and, after 1931, to God. It is possible that his long apprenticeship in serving a demanding woman did more for his soul than all his reading. He would later write with unusual insight about the small daily irritations of family life, about the temptation to resent those we live with, and about the way charity is learned at home or not at all.

Visiting the Widow

The verse at the head of this chapter defines pure religion in two ways: caring for the fatherless and the widow, and keeping oneself unspotted from the world. Mrs Moore was not a widow in 1919, and Maureen was not fatherless, but in every practical sense they had been abandoned, and Paddy’s death had taken their last support. A young atheist undergraduate took them in and kept them. He was not, then, practising religion of any kind. But James would have recognised what he was doing. And when Lewis did become a Christian, he did not end the arrangement or try to escape from it. He went on visiting the widow in her affliction, for twenty more years, until she died.

fields.title: Three Firsts and a Fellowship
fields.body_html:
“And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.”

— Colossians 3:23, KJV

The Oxford Course

The Oxford that Lewis came back to in 1919 was crowded with ex-servicemen, older than the usual undergraduates, many of them carrying wounds of body or mind, all of them in a hurry to make up for lost years. Lewis was one of them. He read Literae Humaniores, the great Oxford course in Greek and Latin literature, ancient history and philosophy, which was taken in two parts. In March 1920 he took a First in the first part, Honour Moderations. In 1921 he won the Chancellor’s English Essay Prize. In the summer of 1922 he took a First in the second part, known as Greats.

That should have been enough to secure him a college fellowship, but in the early 1920s fellowships in philosophy were scarce, and none came. So, with Albert’s reluctant financial support, Lewis took the unusual step of reading a third degree, in English language and literature, which he completed in a single year. In July 1923 he took a First in that too. It was a formidable record, and it made him one of the best-qualified young scholars in Oxford.

It did not immediately make him employed. For two more years he lived on very little, examining, marking papers and writing, while the Moore household scraped along. In 1924 he was given a temporary post teaching philosophy at University College, standing in for a tutor who was away for a year. He applied for one fellowship after another and was turned down. His diary from these years records constant anxiety about money and about his future, and a good deal of quiet desperation.

Friends of the Mind

These were also the years in which Lewis made several of the friendships that shaped his life. Owen Barfield, a young man of brilliant and original mind, had come up to Wadham College after the war, and he and Lewis became close friends. Barfield was a poet and a philosopher of language, and in the early 1920s he became a follower of Rudolf Steiner’s anthroposophy, a kind of spiritual philosophy that Lewis found repellent. The two argued about it for years, in letters and in long walks, in what Lewis jokingly called their Great War. Lewis learned an enormous amount from Barfield, above all the habit of questioning the modern assumption that whatever is newer must be truer. Barfield later became Lewis’s solicitor and the trustee of his charitable fund, and he outlived him by more than thirty years.

There was also Nevill Coghill, a fellow student in the English school, whom Lewis met in a discussion class and was astonished to discover was both the cleverest man in the room and a Christian. There was Cecil Harwood, another follower of Steiner. And there was A. K. Hamilton Jenkin, who taught him to enjoy things for exactly what they were, the ugly and dismal as well as the beautiful. One after another, the most interesting people Lewis met seemed to him to be either Christians or seriously spiritual seekers. He noticed it, and it disturbed him.

Magdalen

In May 1925 Lewis was elected a Fellow of Magdalen College, as tutor in English Language and Literature. Magdalen was, and is, one of the most beautiful colleges in Oxford, with a great medieval bell tower, a deer park and, behind the college, a path called Addison’s Walk that runs around a water meadow between branches of the River Cherwell. Lewis was given a set of rooms in the eighteenth-century New Building, overlooking the deer park on one side and the cloisters on the other. He kept those rooms for nearly thirty years.

Albert was overjoyed. For all the strain between them, his son’s success meant more to him than almost anything. Jack, for his part, wrote his father a long and grateful letter acknowledging all that Albert had done to make it possible. It is one of the warmest letters he ever sent him. It still said nothing about Mrs Moore.

The Tutor

Lewis was a demanding tutor. Each week his pupils came to his rooms, one or two at a time, read him an essay, and then had it taken apart. Some found him intimidating, even crushing. He had learned his methods from Kirkpatrick, and he did not believe in flattering anyone. Others found him the best teacher they ever had. He took their work seriously, he made them think, and once the argument was over he was warm, funny and generous with his time. John Betjeman, the future poet laureate, was one of his early pupils, and the two disliked each other heartily. Others, like George Sayer and the future literary scholars who passed through his rooms, became lifelong friends.

His lectures, on medieval and Renaissance literature, became famous. He lectured without notes, in a loud, clear voice, with enormous learning lightly worn, and his hall was often full. He loved the old books, and he made his hearers love them. He had begun, too, to write the scholarly work that would make his name among his colleagues: a study of the allegorical love poetry of the Middle Ages, which would take him ten years to finish.

Tolkien

On 11 May 1926, at a meeting of the English faculty at Merton College, Lewis met a new professor of Anglo-Saxon, John Ronald Reuel Tolkien. His first impressions, recorded in his diary, were not warm. Tolkien was smooth, pale and fluent, and he held views about the English syllabus that Lewis thought wrong. But Tolkien also loved the northern myths that Lewis had loved since boyhood, and before long Lewis joined a club Tolkien had founded, the Kolbítar, or Coalbiters, whose members met to read the Icelandic sagas in the original. The friendship grew slowly and then fast. By 1929 the two men were sitting up late in Lewis’s rooms, talking about gods and heroes and the old stories, and Tolkien had begun to show Lewis the poems and tales of his own invented mythology.

Tolkien was a devout Roman Catholic. He had lost his mother when he was twelve, and had been brought up by a priest. He did not argue Lewis into faith; argument was not his way. But he took the Christian faith as utterly serious and utterly real, and he took myth seriously too, and he could not see why the two should be kept apart. In time that conviction would be the key that turned the lock.

As to the Lord

The verse at the head of this chapter tells servants to work heartily, as to the Lord. Lewis in the 1920s did not work as to the Lord. He worked for his own advancement, for the pleasure of the work, and for the household that depended on him. But he worked heartily, and the habits he formed in these years, of reading everything, writing clearly, preparing thoroughly and treating pupils as minds rather than customers, stayed with him. When he became a Christian, he did not need to learn how to work. He only needed to learn for whom.

fields.title: Hunted
fields.body_html:
“Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?”

— Psalm 139:7, KJV

The Defences Fall

When Lewis told the story of his conversion in Surprised by Joy, he did not describe it as a search. He described it as a pursuit, with himself as the quarry. Through the second half of the 1920s, he said, his defences fell one by one, and each time he retreated to a new position, he found that it too was untenable. It is worth following the retreat, briefly, because it shows the kind of man he was.

He had begun the decade as a materialist, believing that nothing existed but matter and energy. His philosophy studies, and his long arguments with Barfield, persuaded him that this view could not account for reason itself, for if our thoughts were only the by-products of atoms in motion, there was no reason to trust them, including the thought that materialism was true. So he became a kind of idealist, believing in an Absolute Mind behind the universe, but a mind that made no demands and could not be prayed to. That was comfortable. It asked nothing of him.

Then the Absolute began to look less like a philosopher’s abstraction and more like a Person. His reading kept betraying him. He read George Herbert and found that Herbert seemed to understand life better than any modern writer, and that the understanding came through his faith. He read Chesterton’s The Everlasting Man, published in 1925, and found for the first time an outline of history from a Christian point of view that made sense. He reread the old poets and found that the ones he loved most were Christians, and the ones who agreed with him seemed thin.

The Hardest Atheist

Early in 1926 there was an evening Lewis never forgot. One of the most hard-headed men he knew, a philosopher and atheist named T. D.
