fields.body_html:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.”

— John 1:14, KJV

A Theist in Church

For more than a year after his surrender, Lewis lived as a theist. He prayed, he went to church, he read the Gospels, and he tried to obey his conscience. What he could not do was believe in Christ. The doctrines of the Christian faith, the incarnation, the cross and the resurrection, seemed to him at best puzzling and at worst meaningless. He could not see how the death of a man in Palestine nineteen hundred years ago could have anything to do with him now. Above all he could not understand the doctrine of the atonement: in what sense could the death of one man take away the sins of another?

In his letters to Arthur Greeves, now a believer of a gentle and rather uncertain kind, Lewis discussed these questions honestly. He also began to discuss them with his friends at Oxford. He was, in his own way, still looking. But this time he was looking in the right direction, and he was no longer running away.

The Night of 19 September 1931

On Saturday 19 September 1931, Lewis invited two friends to dine with him at Magdalen. One was Tolkien. The other was Hugo Dyson, a lecturer in English at the University of Reading, a quick, witty, exuberant man and a Christian. After dinner the three went out into the night and walked along Addison’s Walk, the path beside the Cherwell that runs around the water meadow behind the college. They talked for hours. The subject was myth.

What they said was reconstructed afterwards from Lewis’s letters to Greeves and from a poem Tolkien later wrote about the conversation. Lewis loved myths. He loved the old stories of Balder, of Adonis, of Osiris, of the god who dies and comes back to life, and when he met them in pagan literature they moved him profoundly. He did not ask what they meant. He felt their meaning without being able to put it into words. But when he met the same pattern in the Gospels, he demanded explanations, and the explanations he was offered seemed thin.

Tolkien and Dyson turned this around. Why, they asked, should Lewis not approach the story of Christ in the same way he approached the pagan myths, letting it move him and mean something to him before he could explain it? And then they made the decisive point. The story of Christ, they said, was a myth like the others, with all their power and beauty, but with one immense difference: it had really happened. The dying and rising God had come, in history, at a particular time and in a particular place, under a particular Roman governor, and the pagan stories had been dim anticipations of the true one. God had told the story not in words but in events. The myth had become fact.

Lewis listened, argued, and listened again. At about three in the morning Tolkien went home. Lewis and Dyson walked on and talked until nearly four.

The Ride to Whipsnade

Lewis did not become a Christian that night. But the conversation had removed the barrier that had stood between him and faith. He had understood that he could approach the Gospels as he approached the myths he loved, and that their meaning did not depend on his being able to explain it all in advance.

Nine days later, on Monday 28 September 1931, Warnie drove Jack to Whipsnade Zoo, which had opened in Bedfordshire that year. Warnie was on leave from the army, and he had a motorcycle with a sidecar. It was a sunny morning. Jack sat in the sidecar. What happened on the journey was not the result of a new argument, or even of conscious thought. As he put it in Surprised by Joy: “When we set out I did not believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and when we reached the zoo I did.” He compared it to waking: one becomes aware that one is already awake, without remembering the moment it happened.

This book follows the date most biographers give for the ride, 28 September, which fits the dates of Lewis’s letters. One or two accounts give an earlier day the same month. Like the question of 1929 or 1930, it changes the timing and not the story.

The Letters to Arthur

On 1 October 1931 Lewis wrote to Arthur Greeves. He told him, quite simply, that he now believed not only in God but in Christ, and that his long night talk with Dyson and Tolkien had had a great deal to do with it. A few weeks later he wrote again, at much greater length, explaining what had changed. He had come to see the story of Christ as a true myth, and to see that the doctrines the church drew from it were human attempts to translate into concepts what God had already expressed in a more real language, in actual events. He did not yet understand everything. He was certain only that he believed.

Warnie, Too

There was a second conversion in the family that year, and it is sometimes forgotten. Warnie, who had drifted away from faith much as Jack had, though with less philosophy, had been making his own quiet way back. In the spring of 1931, while serving with the army in England, he began to pray again and found that he believed. By the end of that year both brothers were believers again, and from then on they shared the faith as they had shared everything else since the nursery. When Warnie came home for good, the brothers worshipped together at Holy Trinity.

Christmas Day 1931

On Christmas Day 1931, Lewis took Communion at Holy Trinity Church in Headington Quarry, the parish church near the house where the household had moved the year before. It was his first Communion since the miserable confirmation of 1914. This time he believed. He remained a faithful communicant of the Church of England for the rest of his life, and he was buried in that same churchyard.

The Word Made Flesh

The verse at the head of this chapter is the heart of what Lewis came to believe on Addison’s Walk. The Word, the eternal reason and meaning of the universe, did not remain an idea. He became flesh, and he lived among us, and he was seen. For a man who had spent his life loving stories of gods and doubting that any of them were true, it was the most astonishing news in the world. All his longings, all his love of myth, all his rigour of mind, were not contradicted by the Gospel but fulfilled in it. Lewis spent the rest of his life trying to tell others what he had seen that night. The companion volume to this book describes how he told it. This book records simply that, at thirty-two, in a sidecar on the road to a zoo, he came home.

fields.title: The Kilns
fields.body_html:
“Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.”

— Psalm 127:1, KJV

A House on the Hill

After Albert’s death, Little Lea was sold, and the brothers divided what their father had left them. With his share, and with money of Mrs Moore’s from a legacy, Lewis was able to do something the household had never been able to do before: buy a home. In the summer of 1930 they found one. It was a low, brick house built on the site of an old brickworks at the foot of Shotover Hill, about three miles east of Oxford, in the hamlet of Headington Quarry. Two old kilns stood beside it, and gave the house its name. It came with eight acres of woodland, a large overgrown garden, and a flooded clay pit that had become a pond. Lewis loved it at first sight.

The Kilns cost £3,300. Mrs Moore paid the largest part and the brothers the rest, and the house was bought in her name, with Jack and Warnie each having the right to live there for life. After their deaths it was to pass to Maureen. The household moved in on 10 October 1930. Lewis lived there for the next thirty-three years, and he died there.

The Household

It was never a quiet house. Mrs Moore ran it, with a succession of maids and helpers whom she was apt to quarrel with and dismiss. Maureen, by then in her twenties and training as a music teacher, lived there until her marriage in 1940. A gardener and handyman named Fred Paxford joined the household in 1930 and stayed for more than thirty years. Paxford was a gloomy, kindly countryman who always expected the worst and was usually cheerful about it. He became a fixture of Lewis’s life, and there were dogs, cats and at one point a large number of hens.

In December 1932 Warnie retired from the army after eighteen years’ service, as a captain, and came home for good. He was recalled to the colours in 1939 and served briefly in France before being sent home again in 1940, by then a major, and Major Lewis he remained. He was given his own rooms at the Kilns, and he settled into a life of reading, walking, gardening and writing. Over the next few years he sorted and typed out the whole mass of the Lewis family papers, letters and diaries going back to the nineteenth century, into eleven bound volumes. Later he wrote several well-received books on the history of seventeenth-century France, his own great interest. And from the 1940s onwards he served, without pay, as his brother’s secretary.

The arrangement was not always easy. Warnie and Mrs Moore disliked each other. He thought her tyrannical and she thought him idle. He took refuge in his books and in long walks, and sometimes in drink. Jack stood between them and tried to keep the peace. But the brothers were together again, as they had been as boys at Little Lea, and for both of them that counted for more than the friction.

The Pond and the Woods

Lewis loved the grounds of the Kilns. He swam in the pond in all weathers, sometimes punting a flat-bottomed boat across it. He walked in the woods every day. He knew the birds and the trees, and he cleared paths through the undergrowth. Friends who visited remembered him striding about in old clothes, a pipe in his mouth, talking at full speed. It was a quiet, almost rural life only three miles from the city, and it suited him. Many of the landscapes of his later stories have something of the Kilns about them: the woods, the water, the sense of an ordinary English place on the edge of something wild.

Holy Trinity

From the Kilns, Holy Trinity Church was a short walk across the fields. It was a plain Victorian village church built for the quarrymen of Headington, and it became Lewis’s parish church for the rest of his life. He went to the early service of Holy Communion on Sunday mornings, usually at eight, and he sat in a pew near the front, at the side, where he could see the altar and be seen by very few. He did not stay for the later, sung service, because he disliked hymns. He was a faithful, regular, undemonstrative member of the congregation. In time the vicar, the congregation and the village came to know him not as a famous author but as Mr Lewis from the Kilns, who came early, slipped away quickly, and gave generously and quietly to the parish.

The First Christian Book

The first book Lewis wrote as a Christian was written in a fortnight. In August 1932, staying with Arthur Greeves at his home near Belfast, he wrote an allegory of his own journey to faith, modelled on John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress. It was published in 1933 as The Pilgrim’s Regress. It is not one of his best books. It is too clever, too full of private allusions, and some of its satire is bitter. Lewis himself later thought it was needlessly obscure and uncharitable. But it shows how quickly he set out to put his faith into writing, and how naturally he turned to Bunyan, the tinker of Bedford whom he admired all his life.

His scholarly work went on alongside. In 1936 he published The Allegory of Love, the study of medieval love poetry he had been writing for a decade. It made his name at once among literary scholars and won a major prize. It remains a classic of its field. In 1938 he published his first novel, Out of the Silent Planet, a story of a voyage to Mars. A great deal of Christian thought was hidden inside it, and Lewis was amused to discover that hardly any reviewer noticed.

Unless the Lord Build

The verse at the head of this chapter is a warning to builders. The household at the Kilns was not, on any ordinary reckoning, well built. It was a strange collection of people: an Oxford don, his retired brother, an older woman who was not his mother, her grown daughter, a gloomy gardener and a stream of maids. Its tempers were frayed and its peace was uncertain. Yet it lasted for more than twenty years, and out of it came a stream of books that have been read by millions. Lewis would have been the first to say that it was not his skill as a householder that kept it together. He prayed for that house, and he served it, and he trusted that the Lord was building it even when the builders were at odds. He was right.

It was a strange collection of people: an Oxford don, his retired brother, an older woman who was not his mother, her grown daughter, a gloomy gardener and a stream of maids. Its tempers were frayed and its peace was uncertain. Yet it lasted for more than twenty years, and out of it came a stream of books that have been read by millions. Lewis would have been the first to say that it was not his skill as a householder that kept it together. He prayed for that house, and he served it, and he trusted that the Lord was building it even when the builders were at odds. He was right.

fields.title: Thursday Evenings
fields.body_html:
“Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.”

— Malachi 3:16, KJV

The Inklings

Some time in the early 1930s, a small group of friends began to meet in Lewis’s rooms at Magdalen on Thursday evenings. Nobody planned it. The name was borrowed from an undergraduate literary club at University College that had invited Tolkien and Lewis to some of its meetings; when the club died, the name passed to the friends. It was a pun, Tolkien later explained, on people with vague ideas and on people who dabbled in ink. They called themselves the Inklings.

The membership shifted over the years, but its core was always Lewis, his brother Warnie and Tolkien. Others came often: Hugo Dyson, when he was in Oxford; Owen Barfield, when he could get away from his London law practice; Nevill Coghill; a doctor named Robert Havard, who looked after Lewis’s health and that of his household and whom the others called Humphrey; Adam Fox, the dean of divinity at Magdalen; and, later, Tolkien’s son Christopher and others. They were all men, nearly all Christians, and nearly all scholars or writers. Most of them were, in one way or another, at odds with the fashions of the literary world of their day.

The pattern was simple. On Thursday nights, after dinner, they gathered in Lewis’s sitting room. Warnie made tea. Someone produced a manuscript and read from it aloud: a chapter, a poem, a paper. The others criticised it, sometimes kindly and sometimes savagely. Then the talk ranged wherever it went, often until late at night. On Tuesday mornings, or later Monday mornings, a group of the same friends met for an hour or so in a pub on St Giles called the Eagle and Child, which they called the Bird and Baby. There they talked and drank beer and did not read manuscripts.

What Was Read There

An enormous amount of twentieth-century literature was first heard in those rooms. Tolkien read most of The Lord of the Rings to the Inklings, chapter by chapter, over more than a decade. Lewis read his own novels, his books of theology, and some of the letters of a senior devil. Warnie read his chapters on the court of Louis XIV. Charles Williams read his poems and his novels. Lewis was the group’s centre. It was his rooms they met in, his enthusiasm that drove them, his voice that dominated the talk. Tolkien said more than once that without Lewis’s encouragement he would never have finished his great book. Lewis was its first and most devoted reader.

Not everyone was so enthusiastic. Dyson, famously, could not bear Tolkien’s elves and did not hide it. Friendship among the Inklings was robust, and nobody expected to be spared. Lewis valued exactly that. He thought that real friends were people who loved the same truth and were looking at the same thing together, not people who flattered each other. Years later he would write a book in which he described friendship among the loves, and the Thursday evenings at Magdalen were the experience behind that chapter.

Charles Williams

In 1936 Lewis read a novel called The Place of the Lion by an author named Charles Williams, an editor at the Oxford University Press in London. He was so excited by it that he wrote to Williams to say so. By a coincidence that both men enjoyed, Williams had just read the proofs of Lewis’s The Allegory of Love at the press, and had been about to write to Lewis in the same terms. The two letters crossed. A friendship began at once.

Williams was a strange and remarkable man. He came from a poor London family, had left university without a degree, and had worked at the Press since before the First World War. He wrote poetry, plays, theology and a series of what he called spiritual thrillers, novels in which the supernatural breaks into ordinary London life. He had a burning, almost hypnotic personality, and many who met him felt that he lived closer to the unseen world than anyone they knew. He also had an unconventional private life, and in his younger years he had been involved with an occult society, the kind of thing that Lewis normally distrusted. Later scholars have uncovered aspects of his relationships with young women that trouble many readers today, though the Inklings seem to have known little of them.

In September 1939, when war broke out, the Oxford University Press moved its London office to Oxford to escape the expected bombing, and Williams moved with it. For the next six years he was in Oxford, and he became one of the most important figures in Lewis’s life. Lewis arranged for him to lecture in the university, which was an unusual honour for a man without a degree, and his lectures on Milton were a sensation. He came to the Thursday evenings and the Tuesday mornings. He talked theology with Lewis late into the night. He also gave Lewis an idea that would matter to him greatly in the last years of his life: that Christians can, in a real sense, carry one another’s burdens, so that one may bear in love some part of another’s suffering or fear. Williams called it the doctrine of substitution, or coinherence.

15 May 1945

The war in Europe ended on 8 May 1945. A week later, on Tuesday 15 May, Lewis called at the Radcliffe Infirmary on his way to the usual morning meeting, meaning to leave a book or a message for Charles Williams, who had been taken into hospital a few days before. He was told that Williams had just died after an operation. He was fifty-eight. Lewis went on to the Eagle and Child and told the others.

It was the first great loss of Lewis’s adult life since his father’s death, and it struck him hard. And yet, as he wrote to friends at the time, he found that his faith was strengthened rather than shaken by it. He felt, in a way he could not explain, that Williams was not lost, and that the idea of the next life had become more real to him, not less. Two years later he edited a volume of essays by Williams’s friends, among them Dorothy L. Sayers, Tolkien and Barfield, as a tribute to him.

The Book of Remembrance

The verse at the head of this chapter is from Malachi, the last of the prophets. In a cynical and faithless age, a few people who feared the Lord met and talked together, and God listened, and a book of remembrance was written before him. It is a fine description of the Inklings at their best. They were a handful of Christian friends in a sceptical university, reading their work to one another and talking about the things of God. They were not a church and they were not saints. But God hearkened, and books were written in those rooms that are still being read in a hundred languages.

fields.title: A Voice on the Wireless
fields.body_html:
“But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear.”

— 1 Peter 3:15, KJV

Evacuees at the Kilns

When war came again in September 1939, Lewis was forty. He was too old to fight, and his wounds would have excused him anyway, but the war reached the Kilns at once. Within days a group of schoolgirls evacuated from London arrived to live there, and over the next years a succession of evacuee children passed through the house. Lewis, a bachelor who had very little to do with children and claimed not to like them, found that he rather enjoyed them. He also joined the Home Guard, and took his turn, every week or so, patrolling the streets of Oxford with a rifle in the small hours, which he described in letters as a mixture of boredom, cold and unexpectedly good conversation.

Warnie was recalled to the army and sent to France. He came back after the evacuation of the British army in 1940 and was retired again. The household settled down to rationing, blackout and anxiety, like every household in Britain.

The Problem of Pain

Before the war began, a publisher named Ashley Sampson had asked Lewis to write a short book on the problem of suffering for a series of popular Christian books. Lewis agreed, and wrote it during the first winter of the war, reading the chapters aloud to the Inklings as he went. The Problem of Pain was published in October 1940, and dedicated to them. It is a closely argued book, written for readers who wanted to know how a good and all-powerful God could allow the world to suffer as it did. In a country waiting to be bombed, there were a great many such readers. It sold well and was reprinted again and again, and it made Lewis’s name outside the university for the first time.

Screwtape

On a Sunday in July 1940, Lewis was sitting in Holy Trinity Church during the service when an idea came to him for a book. It would be a series of letters from an experienced devil to a junior devil, a nephew who was trying to tempt a young man in England away from God. Everything in it would be upside down: God would be the Enemy, and vice and despair the goal. Lewis wrote to Warnie about the idea that week.

The letters appeared one at a time in an Anglican weekly paper, The Guardian, from May to November 1941. The editor paid Lewis two pounds for each one. Lewis refused the money and had it sent instead to a fund for the widows of clergy. In February 1942 the letters were published as a book, The Screwtape Letters, dedicated to Tolkien. It was an immediate and enormous success. It was reprinted eight times in its first year, and it has never been out of print since. It is the book that first made Lewis famous on both sides of the Atlantic. Lewis himself found it a strain. It had come to him easily, but he later admitted that living for months inside the mind of a devil had been a dry and stifling experience, and he refused for years to write any more.

The BBC

Among the readers of The Problem of Pain was the Reverend James Welch, the director of religious broadcasting at the BBC. In February 1941 he wrote to Lewis asking whether he would give some talks on the radio. Lewis hesitated, then agreed. He was coached in the new art of broadcasting by a BBC producer, the Presbyterian minister Eric Fenn, who taught him to write for the ear: shorter sentences, plainer words, one idea at a time.

The first talk went out on Wednesday 6 August 1941, at a quarter to eight in the evening, for fifteen minutes. It was the beginning of four series of talks over the next three years. The first series asked whether there is any real standard of right and wrong, and what it might tell us about the universe. The second explained what Christians believe. The third was about Christian behaviour, and the fourth about the doctrine of God. Lewis spoke in a deep, unhurried, slightly gruff voice with no clerical solemnity at all. He sounded like an intelligent man talking sense across a kitchen table. Listeners all over the country, many of whom had never heard the faith explained without pious language, wrote to him in their hundreds.

Lewis did not like broadcasting, and he did not like the fame it brought him. He had to travel to London, often at night, through the blackout and the bombing, to speak live into a microphone. He was paid modestly. But he thought that the talks were a duty. The country was at war; many of its people did not know what the faith they were defending was; and he had been asked. The talks were published as three short books and, in 1952, gathered into one volume as Mere Christianity, which has led countless readers to faith.

The Royal Air Force

At about the same time, Lewis was invited by the chaplaincy of the Royal Air Force to speak to airmen at bases around the country. He gave his first talk at the RAF station at Abingdon, near Oxford, in the spring of 1941, and he went on giving them for several years, travelling to stations all over Britain during the university vacations. It was hard work. The audiences were made up of men who had been ordered to attend, many of them tired, sceptical or bored, and many of them knew that they would very likely be killed within months. Lewis felt that the first talks were failures. He was not used to audiences who had not chosen to hear him, and he found it difficult to speak to men whose education and experience were so different from his own.

He learned. He came to think of the RAF talks as a hard but invaluable school. He had to drop his learned allusions, translate every theological term into plain English, and take seriously the questions of men who had no time for anything that sounded like a sermon. It was, he thought, an exercise in humility, and it made him a better apologist.

The Weight of Glory

There were other invitations. On 8 June 1941 he preached at evensong in the university church of St Mary the Virgin, in Oxford, to a congregation that filled the church and spilled out into the street. The sermon was published as The Weight of Glory, and many readers think it the finest thing he ever wrote. In February 1943 he gave a series of lectures at the University of Durham that became The Abolition of Man. In the same years he wrote two more novels of other planets and a dream-fantasy of a bus ride from hell to heaven. The war years were the most productive of his life.

Ready Always to Give an Answer

The verse at the head of this chapter is Peter’s charge to Christians to be ready to give a reason for their hope. It has been called the charter of Christian apologetics, and Lewis took it as a description of his own vocation. But it is worth noticing the last three words: with meekness and fear. Lewis was not always meek. In argument he could be overbearing, and he knew it. But he did treat his hearers, whether airmen in a hut or listeners in a kitchen, with respect. He did not talk down to them. He took their objections seriously because he had once made them himself. And he gave his answers in fear, in the old sense of the word: in reverence before the God he was speaking about, and in the knowledge that he too would give account.

fields.title: A Rule of Life
fields.body_html:
“Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.”

— James 5:16, KJV

Fame and Its Dangers

By 1941 Lewis was becoming famous, and he knew the danger. He was a proud man by temperament, and he had always enjoyed winning arguments. Now thousands of strangers were writing to tell him that he had changed their lives. It is a hard thing for any man to hear, and harder for one who had spent his youth wanting to be thought clever. Lewis feared, rightly, that the success of his Christian books could become a trap: that he might become an expert on religion and stop being a Christian, or that his pride might feed on the very work he was doing for God.

He did several things about it. They are less often told than the story of his books, but they are at least as important to understanding his life.

Father Walter Adams

In October 1940 Lewis began going to confession. He chose as his confessor an elderly priest of the Society of St John the Evangelist, an Anglican religious order whose members were known as the Cowley Fathers, after the district of east Oxford where their mother house stood. Father Walter Adams was then over seventy. He was a quiet, unremarkable-looking man, much sought after as a spiritual director, who had been a parish priest before joining the Society during the First World War. Those who knew him spoke of his humility, his gentleness and his complete absence of fuss.

The decision did not come easily. Lewis admitted in a letter that he dreaded it, and that what might seem a small step to others was a very large one for him. Afterwards he found that it had done him good. He went on going, almost every week, for the next twelve years, until Father Adams died in 1952. It was, by any standard, an extraordinary discipline for a busy Oxford don in the middle of a war, and it was a sign of how seriously he took his own sins.

Confession to a priest was not, and is not, common among English Protestants, and many evangelical readers will find it strange. Lewis did not regard it as necessary for every Christian, and he never urged it on others. He seems to have chosen it because he knew his own heart and did not trust himself to deal with it alone. He needed someone outside himself who would hear the worst, not be impressed by his fame, and tell him the truth. Father Adams did that, and by every account he did it without fuss, pointing his penitent away from himself to Christ.

Prayer

Under Father Adams’s direction, Lewis’s life of prayer became regular and disciplined. He said the daily offices of the Prayer Book, morning and evening prayer, when he could, often in his college chapel or alone in his rooms. He read the Psalms through, as the Prayer Book appoints, month by month. He made his Communion at least once a week, and when he could more often. And he prayed by name for a great many people. As his correspondence grew, so did his list. By the end of his life it was very long, and it included people he had never met, who had written to him for help and whom he had promised to remember. He took those promises seriously. When he told a stranger that he would pray for them, he did.

He was honest, too, about the dryness of prayer. Some of his most helpful letters to correspondents were about the times when prayer felt like talking to an empty room, and about going on anyway. He knew those times well. He did not think that feelings were a reliable measure of prayer, and he had learned at Wynyard what damage could be done by trying to manufacture them. fields.body_html:
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”

— 1 Thessalonians 5:21, KJV

Stella Aldwinckle’s Idea

In the autumn of 1941 a woman named Stella Aldwinckle, who worked as a chaplain to women students for the Oxford Pastorate, an evangelical ministry in the university, had an idea. She had noticed that many students had honest questions about the Christian faith and nowhere to ask them. The religious societies in Oxford were for believers. The atheist and secular societies were for unbelievers. There was no place where the two sides could meet on equal terms and argue the case out in public. She decided to start one, and she asked Lewis to be its president.

Lewis agreed with enthusiasm. It was exactly the kind of thing he loved. The new society was named the Socratic Club, after the Greek philosopher who had taught that one should follow the argument wherever it leads. Its first meeting was held in January 1942. Its rule was simple. At each meeting a speaker would read a paper, and someone from the other side would reply, or the other way round, and then the floor was open. Christians were to hear the strongest case against their faith, and unbelievers the strongest case for it. Lewis was president for twelve years, until he left for Cambridge in 1954.

The Meetings

The club met on Monday evenings during term, usually in a college common room, and the meetings were often crowded. Students sat on the floor and stood in the doorway. The speakers included some of the most distinguished philosophers, scientists and theologians in Britain, believers and unbelievers alike. Lewis read papers himself, replied to others, and took part in the discussion. He was in his element. Those who attended remembered his booming voice, his quickness, his good humour, and his capacity to demolish a careless argument in a sentence.

It was not always comfortable. Some of the unbelieving speakers were very able, and some of the debates went badly for the Christian side. Lewis did not mind that. He thought it was the whole point. A faith that could not stand up to argument was not worth having, and a Christian who had never heard the case against his faith was not ready to defend it. He wanted the club to be fair. He wanted the believers to lose sometimes, if they deserved to.

Miracles

In 1947 Lewis published Miracles, a book arguing that the miracles of the Bible are not ruled out by reason or science. Part of its argument, in the third chapter, was directed against naturalism, the view that nature is all there is. Lewis argued that if naturalism were true, human reasoning would be nothing more than the product of blind physical causes, and we would then have no grounds for trusting it, including the reasoning that led to naturalism. The theory, in other words, cut away the branch it was sitting on.

It was an argument he had held since the 1920s, and he thought it was one of his strongest. The book sold well, and in September 1947 the American news magazine Time put Lewis on its cover. He was by now one of the most famous Christians in the English-speaking world.

2 February 1948

On 2 February 1948, a young philosopher named Elizabeth Anscombe read a paper to the Socratic Club replying to the third chapter of Miracles. She was twenty-eight, a research fellow at Somerville College, a former pupil of the Austrian philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein, and a devout Roman Catholic. She was not attacking Christianity. She was attacking what she considered a bad argument for it. Her criticism was technical. She argued that Lewis had confused two different senses of words like cause and reason, and that his argument against naturalism, as he had stated it, did not work.

By the accounts of those present, it was a sharp and difficult evening. Lewis replied and the discussion went on. Afterwards some who were there thought he had been badly beaten. Lewis himself seems to have agreed that she had made a real point. Over the following years he rewrote the chapter, and in 1960, when a new edition of Miracles was published, the third chapter had been carefully revised to meet her objections.

The Legend

Out of that evening grew a legend that is still often repeated. It holds that Lewis was so humiliated by Anscombe that he lost confidence in reason, gave up writing apologetics, and retreated into children’s stories. A. N. Wilson’s biography gave the story wide currency in 1990.

The legend is mostly false. It is true that Lewis wrote fewer books of direct apologetics after 1948, and true that he took Anscombe’s criticism seriously. But he did not abandon apologetics. He went on presiding over the Socratic Club for six more years, went on lecturing and debating, and went on writing Christian books of many kinds for the rest of his life, including a revised version of the very argument she had criticised. The Narnia books had been in his mind for years before 1948, and he began to write the first of them in earnest in 1948 and 1949 for reasons that had nothing to do with Anscombe. And Anscombe herself, later in life, said that the legend was nonsense. She remembered the meeting as a serious discussion of a definite philosophical point, and she thought Lewis’s revised chapter was a great improvement, though she still had reservations. She also observed, drily, that those who wrote about the occasion as a great defeat seemed to her to be showing more about their own attitudes than about what happened.

What does seem to be true is that the evening left a mark on Lewis. Friends who saw him soon afterwards remembered him as unusually low, and he did not hide from them that he thought he had come off worse. It reminded him that his arguments were not infallible, and that he could be wrong. He may well have concluded that the kind of apologetics he had done during the war had served its time, and that other kinds of writing would now reach people better. But that is a long way from a crisis of faith.

Prove All Things

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s instruction to test everything and to keep what is good. It could have been the motto of the Socratic Club. It is also a fair description of how Lewis dealt with his defeat. He tested his own argument, found it wanting, revised it, and kept what was good in it. That is not the behaviour of a man whose faith was shaken. It is the behaviour of a scholar who believed that the truth could survive any honest criticism, and that a Christian should be the first to welcome it. His pride was hurt. His faith was not.

fields.title: The Long Decline
fields.body_html:
“Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”

— Galatians 6:2, KJV

The Hardest Years

The years just after the Second World War were, in public, the summit of Lewis’s fame. In private they were among the hardest of his life. He was exhausted by the war years, in which he had taught, lectured, written, broadcast and travelled without a break. The household at the Kilns was growing more difficult. And the two people he lived with were both, in different ways, falling apart.

Mrs Moore

Janie Moore was in her seventies. She suffered from varicose ulcers in her legs, and she grew steadily less able to move about. She also grew more demanding, more anxious and more querulous. She quarrelled with the maids, worried about everything, and wanted Jack at hand constantly. Visitors to the Kilns in those years remembered seeing Lewis called from his work or his conversation, again and again, to deal with some small domestic crisis: a dog that needed walking, a maid who had given notice, a message, a cup of tea. Warnie’s diary from these years is full of fury at her, and at what he saw as her tyranny over his brother.

Lewis did not complain, at least not often. His letters to friends sometimes speak of the pressure of the household, and he asked one or two close correspondents for their prayers, without going into detail. To most people he said nothing at all. He nursed her, fetched and carried for her, and listened to her. He seems to have thought that this was simply his duty, and that the duty did not lessen because it had become hard.

Warnie

Warnie, meanwhile, was drinking. He had always enjoyed a drink, as most army officers of his generation did, but in the years after the war his drinking became something else. He would go on binges that lasted days or weeks, often when he was away from home or under strain, and he would sometimes end in hospital. In the summer of 1947, on holiday in Ireland, he drank himself into such a state that he was taken into Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital at Drogheda, run by an order of Irish nuns, the Medical Missionaries of Mary. Jack crossed to Ireland to be with him. The nuns nursed Warnie back to health, then and on many later occasions, and he grew deeply attached to them.

Lewis never wrote publicly about his brother’s alcoholism, and he rarely wrote of it privately. He did not lecture or reproach him, at least not in any record that survives. He worried, prayed, fetched him home, and forgave him. The brothers’ love for each other never wavered. But Warnie’s drinking added greatly to the strain of Jack’s life, and there were times when Jack, who depended on his brother more than anyone, could not depend on him at all.

June 1949

In June 1949 Lewis collapsed. He had been working without a holiday for years, he was run down, and he picked up a serious streptococcal infection. He was rushed into the Acland nursing home in Oxford, where he was treated with injections of the new drug penicillin. His doctor, Robert Havard, told Warnie that his brother was dangerously exhausted and needed a complete rest. Warnie, under the strain, began drinking heavily again.

Lewis recovered, but slowly. His friends began to worry seriously about him. Some of them felt that the burden of the household at the Kilns was killing him, and one or two said so. But Lewis would not hear of changing the arrangement. He had made a promise, and he would keep it.

Restholme

In April 1950 the decision was taken out of his hands. Mrs Moore, by then seventy-eight, after a series of falls, could no longer be cared for at home. She was moved to a nursing home in Oxford called Restholme. Lewis visited her almost every day for the rest of her life, often travelling across Oxford in the middle of a heavy working day to sit with her. She was often confused, and the visits cannot always have been easy. He went anyway.

She died on 12 January 1951, of influenza, at the age of seventy-eight. She was buried in the churchyard of Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry, where Jack would one day lie as well. Lewis had kept his promise to Paddy Moore for more than thirty years.

Relief and Grief

What Lewis felt at her death he did not say publicly. To friends he admitted a kind of relief, as anyone who has nursed a long illness will understand, and also real grief. She had been the centre of his household for half his life. She had given him a home when he had none, and whatever else the relationship had been, it had been long and close. Warnie, on the other hand, recorded his relief without any mixture at all. The house became, for a few years, quieter.

Passed Over

In these same years Lewis suffered a series of disappointments in his career. He was by now, by any reasonable measure, one of the most distinguished literary scholars in Oxford, the author of The Allegory of Love and of a stream of other learned work, and the best-attended lecturer in the English faculty. Yet he was never offered a professorship at Oxford. More than once he was passed over for a chair he might reasonably have expected. In 1951 he was a candidate for the elected post of Professor of Poetry, and lost to the poet Cecil Day-Lewis.

Some of his colleagues frankly disapproved of him. They thought that a scholar who wrote popular books about religion, spoke on the radio and was on the cover of an American magazine was not quite respectable. Some were offended by his outspoken faith. Others simply disliked his personality, which could be loud and overbearing in the common room. Lewis felt the slights, but he did not complain about them in public, and there is little bitterness about them in his letters. He had, by then, learned something about humility, and something about not needing the good opinion of the people around him.

The Law of Christ

The verse at the head of this chapter tells Christians to bear one another’s burdens. Lewis bore a great many in these years: an old woman’s decline, a brother’s drinking, a heavy load of teaching, and the letters of thousands of strangers. He did it, for the most part, without being thanked and without telling anyone. It nearly broke his health. But it was in these years, when his life was at its most constricted, that he began to write the books that would carry his name furthest of all.

She was often confused, and the visits cannot always have been easy. He went anyway. She died on 12 January 1951, of influenza, at the age of seventy-eight. She was buried in the churchyard of Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry, where Jack would one day lie as well. Lewis had kept his promise to Paddy Moore for more than thirty years. Relief and Grief What Lewis felt at her death he did not say publicly. To friends he admitted a kind of relief, as anyone who has nursed a long illness will understand, and also real grief. She had been the centre of his household for half his life. She had given him a home when he had none, and whatever else the relationship had been, it had been long and close. Warnie, on the other hand, recorded his relief without any mixture at all. The house became, for a few years, quieter. Passed Over In these same years Lewis suffered a series of disappointments in his career. He was by now, by any reasonable measure, one of the most distinguished literary scholars in Oxford, the author of The Allegory of Love and of a stream of other learned work, and the best-attended lecturer in the English faculty. Yet he was never offered a professorship at Oxford. More than once he was passed over for a chair he might reasonably have expected. In 1951 he was a candidate for the elected post of Professor of Poetry, and lost to the poet Cecil Day-Lewis. Some of his colleagues frankly disapproved of him. They thought that a scholar who wrote popular books about religion, spoke on the radio and was on the cover of an American magazine was not quite respectable. Some were offended by his outspoken faith. Others simply disliked his personality, which could be loud and overbearing in the common room. Lewis felt the slights, but he did not complain about them in public, and there is little bitterness about them in his letters. He had, by then, learned something about humility, and something about not needing the good opinion of the people around him. The Law of Christ The verse at the head of this chapter tells Christians to bear one another’s burdens. Lewis bore a great many in these years: an old woman’s decline, a brother’s drinking, a heavy load of teaching, and the letters of thousands of strangers. He did it, for the most part, without being thanked and without telling anyone. It nearly broke his health. But it was in these years, when his life was at its most constricted, that he began to write the books that would carry his name furthest of all.

fields.title: A Wardrobe and a Chair
fields.body_html:
“Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.”

— Matthew 18:3, KJV

Pictures in His Head

Lewis always said that his stories began not with ideas but with pictures. Since he was about sixteen, he said, he had carried in his mind a picture of a faun carrying an umbrella and parcels through a snowy wood. For many years he did nothing with it. In 1939, when the evacuee children came to the Kilns, he began a story about four children sent away from London who find their way into another world, and wrote a few sentences. Then he put it aside. Nearly ten years later, in 1948 and 1949, he took it up again and finished it.

He read it to Tolkien, who disliked it intensely. Tolkien thought it a hasty jumble of different mythologies, with fauns and Father Christmas and talking beavers all in the same wood, and he said so. Lewis was discouraged but not deterred. He read it to Roger Lancelyn Green, a former pupil who wrote children’s books, and Green loved it. Lewis went on.

The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe was published in October 1950, with illustrations by a young artist named Pauline Baynes. Six more books followed, one a year, until 1956. Together they became The Chronicles of Narnia. The last of them, The Last Battle, won the Carnegie Medal, the highest award for children’s literature in Britain.

This book does not retell them. Lewis insisted that they were not allegories, in which each character stands for something else, but stories in which he imagined what the Son of God might be like if there were another world and he came into it. Readers of every age have found in them the goodness, the terror and the joy of Christ, and they have been read by many tens of millions of children since. Readers who want them should go to the books themselves.

Why Children’s Books?

People were surprised. Lewis was a bachelor in his fifties who had no children of his own and little experience of them. Many of his friends thought it an odd turn. Lewis gave several explanations, in essays written later. He said that the fairy story was simply the best form for what he wanted to say. He said that a story for children could sometimes slip past what he called the watchful dragons: the stiffness and reluctance that many people feel about religion because they were told as children that they ought to feel certain things about God. And he held that a good story for children ought to be one that grown-ups could enjoy as well.

There may also have been a more personal reason. Lewis had lost his own childhood suddenly, at nine, and had spent much of his youth longing for something he could not name. The man who wrote the Narnia books was writing, in a sense, for the boy at Little Lea. He was giving to other children what he would have given anything to have been given himself.

Letters From Children

The children wrote to him. They wrote in thousands, from Britain, America and all over the world, and he answered them. His letters to children are among the most charming things he wrote: patient, funny, never condescending, and always taking their questions seriously. When a child worried that he loved Aslan more than Jesus, Lewis wrote back gently that the child could not really do so, since the things he loved Aslan for were the very things Jesus had done and said.

Cambridge

In 1954 the University of Cambridge created a new chair, the professorship of Medieval and Renaissance English, and the electors offered it to Lewis. He at first declined. He did not want to leave the Kilns or Warnie, and he did not think he could manage the move. The electors, among them his friend Tolkien, persisted, and the college to which the chair was attached, Magdalene, offered him a fellowship and rooms. It was arranged that he could spend the week in Cambridge during term and come home to the Kilns at weekends. In June 1954 he accepted.

It was the recognition that Oxford had never given him, and it made a great difference to his life. On 29 November 1954, his fifty-sixth birthday, he gave his inaugural lecture in Cambridge to a crowded hall. In it he argued that the great divide in the history of Western culture was not between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, as most scholars thought, but between the whole of the old Christian world and the modern one, and he presented himself, half jokingly, as a surviving specimen of the older kind. On 1 January 1955 he moved into his rooms at Magdalene.

He was happy at Cambridge. The atmosphere was kinder than at Oxford, and he found his new colleagues welcoming. He had no undergraduates to tutor, only lectures to give and research students to supervise, and after thirty years of tutorials it was a great release. Magdalene, a small, friendly, rather old-fashioned college, suited him well. He spent the week there during term and went home to Oxford by the slow cross-country train at the weekends.

Two Books of 1955 and 1956

In 1955 Lewis published Surprised by Joy, the account of his early life and conversion. He had been working on it for years. Its title, taken from a sonnet of Wordsworth, named the longing he had known since childhood. His friends would soon enjoy the joke that he was about to be surprised by a Joy of quite another kind. In 1956 he published Till We Have Faces, a retelling of an ancient myth, which he thought the best book he had written and which most readers at the time ignored. It was dedicated to a woman who had helped him with it: Joy Davidman, an American writer who had been his friend for several years. Their story belongs to the next chapters.

As Little Children

The verse at the head of this chapter is Jesus’ warning that no one enters the kingdom of heaven without becoming like a child. Lewis was the most learned man most people had ever met. He read a dozen languages and knew the whole of European literature. And yet, in his fifties, he turned to writing stories for children, and some of what he most wanted to say he said in them. It is a kind of parable. The scholar who had once thought religion beneath a grown man’s intelligence had learned that the kingdom belongs to those who receive it as children, and he spent the best of his imagination on helping children receive it.

fields.title: Joy Davidman
fields.body_html:
“For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth.”

— Psalm 71:5, KJV

A Girl From the Bronx

Helen Joy Davidman was born in New York City on 18 April 1915, the daughter of Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe. Her father, Joseph Davidman, was a schoolteacher and later a school principal. Her family were not religious, and Joy grew up an atheist. She was astonishingly clever. She went to Hunter College at fifteen, took a master’s degree in English at Columbia University at twenty, and was soon publishing poems, reviews and novels. In 1938 her first book of poems, Letter to a Comrade, won a national prize for young poets, the Yale Series of Younger Poets award, and was published to wide praise.

Like many young American intellectuals of the Depression years, Joy turned to Communism. She joined the Communist Party in 1938, and for several years she wrote for its magazine, New Masses. She went briefly to Hollywood as a scriptwriter, without success. In 1942 she married a fellow Communist and writer, William Lindsay Gresham, who had fought for the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War and who suffered from alcoholism and depression. They had two sons, David, born in 1944, and Douglas, born in 1945. They lived in a house in the country north of New York.

A Night in 1946

The marriage was unhappy from the start. Bill drank, was unfaithful, and was subject to violent moods. One evening in the spring of 1946 he telephoned Joy from New York to say that he was having a breakdown, that he could not come home, and that he did not know what he would do. Then he rang off. Joy was alone in the house with two small children, with no way of reaching him and nothing she could do.

What happened next she described a few years later in an essay she wrote about her conversion. In her helplessness her pride gave way, and for the first time in her life she found that she was aware of God. She did not reason her way to him. She felt that he was there, in the room, and that he had been waiting for her. She found herself on her knees, praying. Bill came home safely, and not long afterwards both of them began attending a Presbyterian church, though Bill’s faith did not last.

Joy had already been reading the books of C. S. Lewis, and after her conversion she read more. She found in them the clearest account she knew of the faith she had stumbled into, and an intellect that matched her own.

The First Letter

In January 1950 she wrote to him. Her early letters have not survived, but Warnie, who handled much of his brother’s post, later recalled that hers stood out from the rest: they were lively, direct and well informed, and their writer was plainly a match for Jack in argument. Lewis replied. A correspondence began that lasted more than two years.

By 1952 Joy’s marriage was in ruins. She was ill and exhausted, and she decided to go to England for a few months, partly to recover, partly to work on a book, and partly, it seems clear, to meet the man whose letters had come to mean so much to her. She left the boys with Bill and with her cousin Renée Pierce, who had come to live with them after leaving a marriage of her own. In August she sailed for England.

The Eastgate Hotel

On 24 September 1952, Lewis met Joy Davidman for the first time, at lunch in the Eastgate Hotel in Oxford, opposite Magdalen. She had come with a friend. The lunch was a success, and it was followed by others, at Magdalen and at the Kilns. Joy was blunt, funny, abrasive and fearless. She said exactly what she thought, she was not in the least overawed by Lewis, and she beat him at his own game of argument. He enjoyed it hugely. Warnie, when he met her, liked her too, and he remained her loyal friend to the end.

That December, Joy spent Christmas at the Kilns. While she was there a letter came from Bill. He told her that he and Renée had fallen in love and asked for a divorce. Joy showed the letter to Lewis, and he advised her to agree. She went back to America in January 1953 to settle her affairs.

London and Headington

In November 1953 Joy came back to England, this time with her sons, and settled in London. She was poor: Bill was supposed to send money, and rarely did. She supported herself and the boys by writing and by occasional work, and Lewis quietly helped to pay the boys’ school fees. Her divorce was granted in 1954. Her book on the Ten Commandments, Smoke on the Mountain, had appeared in America in 1953, and when it was published in Britain in 1955 Lewis wrote a foreword for it.

She and her sons visited the Kilns in the holidays. David and Douglas, then about nine and eight, were enthralled by the house, its woods, its pond, and the tall, kindly professor who had written the Narnia books. In 1955 Joy moved to Headington, to a house in the Old High Street, about a mile from the Kilns. Lewis found it for her and paid the rent.

By then it was obvious to their friends that Joy was in love with Lewis. Whether Lewis was in love with her is much less clear, and he himself seems not to have known for some time. He enjoyed her company more than anyone’s outside the Inklings. He depended on her for criticism and encouragement in his writing. But he was a bachelor of nearly sixty who had never expected to marry, and he seems to have thought of their relationship as a deep friendship and nothing more.

A Wedding of Convenience

In 1956 the British Home Office refused to renew Joy’s permit to live in England. She and her sons would have to return to America. Lewis could not bear the thought of losing her company, and he could see no reason why she and her sons should be sent back to a country where they had no home and very little money. He offered a solution. He would marry her in a civil ceremony, which would give her British nationality and the right to stay. The marriage would be a legal formality only. They would not live together. She would remain at her own house, and he at the Kilns.

On 23 April 1956 C. S. Lewis and Joy Davidman Gresham were married at the register office in St Giles, Oxford. Very few people were told. Lewis did not regard it as a real marriage, since it had not taken place in church, and he expected nothing to change.

Hope From Youth

The verse at the head of this chapter is a prayer of an old man who has trusted God since his youth. Joy Davidman had not trusted God from her youth. She came to him at thirty, as Lewis had come at thirty-two, after years of atheism and against the grain of all her education. Like him, she had been found by a God she had not been looking for. That shared experience was part of what drew them together. They were two converts, two former unbelievers, two people who had spent their lives in argument and had both, at last, knelt down. Neither of them knew, in the spring of 1956, how little time they had.

fields.title: A Bedside Wedding
fields.body_html:
“Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.”

— James 5:14-15, KJV

18 October 1956

For some months in 1956 Joy had been suffering pains in her hip and leg. Her doctor thought it was rheumatism. On the evening of 18 October 1956, her thigh bone snapped. She was taken to the Wingfield-Morris Orthopaedic Hospital in Headington. X-rays showed that the femur had been eaten away by cancer, and further tests found cancer in her breast and in other bones. The doctors did not expect her to live long.

It was this, Lewis afterwards said, that made him understand his own feelings. Faced with the prospect of losing her, he found that what he felt for Joy was not friendship at all, or not only. He was in love with her. The civil marriage, which he had treated as a formality, now seemed to him a mockery: he was legally married to a woman he loved and who was dying, and in the eyes of the Church, and in his own, he was not married to her at all.

Speaking Openly

He began, for the first time, to tell his friends. Some were astonished, some were dismayed, and one or two were hostile. Tolkien in particular seems to have been hurt not to have been told of the civil marriage, and he never warmed to Joy. Warnie, who had known all along, supported his brother completely. On 24 December 1956 a notice appeared in The Times announcing that a marriage had taken place between Professor C. S. Lewis and Mrs Joy Gresham, and asking that no letters be sent.

Joy was moved from one hospital to another, and her treatment was long and painful: operations, radiation and great suffering. Lewis visited her every day he could. When he was in Cambridge, he wrote to her.

The Bishop’s Refusal

Lewis wanted a Christian marriage. But Joy had been divorced, and her former husband was still alive. The Church of England in the 1950s did not marry divorced people in church while a former spouse lived, and the Bishop of Oxford, Harry Carpenter, refused permission for the marriage. Lewis argued that Joy’s first marriage had not been a valid Christian marriage at all, since Bill Gresham had himself been married and divorced before he married her. The bishop was not persuaded. Lewis, who had always been a loyal and obedient churchman, would not go behind his back.

Peter Bide

In March 1957 the doctors told Lewis that Joy had very little time left. Lewis thought of a former pupil of his, Peter Bide, who had become a priest and was serving a parish in Sussex. Bide was said to have been used by God in the healing of a sick child. Lewis asked him to come to Oxford, not to marry them but to lay hands on Joy and pray for her healing.

Bide came. When he arrived and understood the whole situation, he was moved by it. Lewis had not asked him to marry them, but Bide decided that he would. He later explained that, faced with a dying woman and a man who loved her and wanted to be married to her before God, he could not in conscience refuse. He knew that the Bishop of Oxford would not be pleased, and he was right.

21 March 1957

On 21 March 1957, in Joy’s hospital room, Peter Bide married C. S. Lewis and Joy Davidman according to the rites of the Church of England. Warnie was there. Joy could not rise from her bed. After the marriage Bide laid his hands on her and prayed for her healing. Then he went home.

In letters written at the time, Lewis prepared his friends to hear that he would very soon be a widower.

In April Joy was sent home to the Kilns to die, and a nurse came to care for her. Lewis, Warnie, the boys when they were home, and the household gathered round her.

Remission

She did not die. Over the following weeks and months, to the astonishment of her doctors, the cancer stopped advancing. Then it began to recede. The diseased bones started to heal. By the summer she was able to sit up, then to move about the house in a wheelchair, and by the end of the year she could walk with a stick. By 1958 she was strong enough to go out, to visit friends, and to go on holiday. The doctors had no explanation for it. They could only say that remission of that kind sometimes happened, though rarely.

Lewis believed that God had answered prayer, and so did Joy. They did not claim to understand why. Many people had prayed for her, in Oxford and in America and elsewhere, and the prayer Bide had offered at her bedside was one among them. Lewis was careful not to say too much, and he never treated her recovery as a proof of anything. But he was grateful with all his heart.

Something Borne

At the same time, something odd happened to Lewis himself. In the summer of 1957 he began to suffer from severe pain in his back and legs. The doctors found that he had osteoporosis, a loss of calcium from his bones, and he was forced to wear a surgical belt and to give up many of the long walks he loved. As Joy’s bones grew stronger, his grew weaker.

fields.title: Three Years
fields.body_html:
“To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: … A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance.”

— Ecclesiastes 3:1, 4, KJV

A Late Happiness

Lewis was nearly sixty when Joy came home to the Kilns, and he had never expected to be married. He found, to his own amazement, that he was happy in a way he had not been since childhood. He told friends so, simply and without embarrassment. He had not known, he said in effect, that such happiness was possible, and he had certainly not expected it to come to him so late, or in such circumstances.

Joy brought the Kilns to life. The house had been neglected for years. Mrs Moore had not been able to look after it in her last decade, and the two brothers had not much cared. There were holes in the carpets, broken windows, threadbare furniture and damp in the walls. Joy, once she could move about, set about putting it right. She had the house redecorated, the carpets replaced and the heating improved. She took charge of the accounts and of the household staff. She discovered, to her indignation, that poachers and trespassers had been using the Kilns woods for years, and she saw them off. Paxford, who had run the place in his own way for nearly thirty years, did not altogether like the change. Warnie did. He and Joy became firm friends, and he was delighted to see the old house come back to life.

A Marriage of True Minds

The two of them were extraordinarily well matched. Joy was the only person Lewis had ever met, apart from a few of the Inklings, who could argue with him on equal terms, and she did so constantly. She was quick, funny, sharp-tongued and sometimes rude. Several of Lewis’s friends disliked her, and some thought she was bad for him. Others saw that she made him happy, and loved her for it. She helped him with his writing, read his drafts, made suggestions and criticisms, and encouraged him. Lewis said that Till We Have Faces owed a great deal to her, and his later books bear signs of their conversations.

They also prayed together, went to church together, and read together. Joy shared her husband’s faith wholeheartedly. Their marriage was, in the fullest sense, a Christian one.

Ireland

In July 1958, with Joy strong enough to travel, the two of them went to Ireland for a belated honeymoon. It was the first time Lewis had ever flown. They visited Arthur Greeves and other old friends and relatives, and toured the countryside of Lewis’s childhood: the hills and coast of County Down and further afield, as far as Donegal. Lewis showed Joy everything he had loved as a boy, and Joy, who had grown up in the Bronx, loved it too.

Work in Those Years

Lewis went on working. In term he was in Cambridge during the week, and he came home to the Kilns as early as he could on Fridays. In 1958 he published Reflections on the Psalms, a book written for ordinary readers about the difficulties and the delights of praying the Psalms, and in 1960 The Four Loves, a book about affection, friendship, romantic love and charity. In the summer of 1958 he recorded a series of talks on the four loves for an American religious broadcasting organisation. Some American listeners were shocked by his frankness about sex, and the talks were not widely broadcast at the time. He also wrote a sequel to the Screwtape letters, in the form of a toast proposed by the senior devil at a dinner for young tempters, which was published in an American magazine in 1959.

The Cancer Returns

In October 1959 a routine examination at the hospital showed that the cancer had come back. There were new tumours in Joy’s bones. The doctors said that she could be given treatment that might hold it back for a time, but that it would not cure her. Lewis wrote to friends with a heavy heart. They had known it might happen. Knowing did not make it easier.

Greece

Joy had always wanted to see Greece. For a scholar of classical literature like Lewis, it would have been the journey of a lifetime too, and he had never made it. In the spring of 1960, with the doctors’ reluctant agreement, they went. They travelled with two old friends, Roger Lancelyn Green, Lewis’s former pupil, and his wife June. From 3 to 14 April they toured Greece and the islands: Athens, Mycenae, Rhodes, Crete and Knossos. Joy was in pain much of the time and could not walk far, but she was determined to see all she could, and she saw a great deal. Lewis, who had read about these places all his life, saw them at last, with his wife beside him.

Green kept a diary of the trip, and later dedicated his biography of Lewis to the memory of Jack and Joy and of what he called their tour of the Greek islands. Everyone who was there remembered it as a time of great happiness, in spite of everything. It was the last journey Joy ever made.

The End

After their return Joy’s condition grew worse quickly. In the early summer she had a major operation. Early in July she was taken into the Radcliffe Infirmary in Oxford. Lewis was with her as much as he could be. On 13 July 1960 she died, with him at her side. She was forty-five.

Before she died she received absolution from Austin Farrer, one of the most distinguished theologians in England, who had become a close friend of them both. Lewis afterwards told friends that at the end she had been at peace with God. Her body was cremated at the Oxford crematorium, where Farrer took the funeral service, and her ashes were scattered in the rose garden there. Lewis wrote a short poem for her memorial plaque, which can still be read there.

A Time to Dance

The verse at the head of this chapter speaks of the seasons God appoints for every purpose: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. Lewis and Joy had been given a time to dance. It lasted a little over three years after the bedside wedding, and four from the day in the register office. It was brief, and it was overshadowed from beginning to end by the knowledge of her illness. But they took it as a gift, and they were glad in it. When it ended, the time to weep began, and Lewis entered it more completely than he had ever entered anything.

fields.title: A Grief Observed
fields.body_html:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?”

— Psalm 22:1, KJV

The Notebooks

In the weeks after Joy’s death, Lewis did what he had always done with experience: he wrote it down. He had found some old exercise books in the house, and in them, almost every day, he set down what he was feeling and thinking. He did not write for publication. He seems to have written partly to keep himself from going under, and partly because writing was the only way he knew to look at something clearly. He filled four notebooks. Then he stopped, because he had run out of notebooks, and because he found that he had come to the end of something.

The first sentence of the first notebook has become one of the most quoted sentences he ever wrote. “No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear.” What follows is not a treatise on suffering. Lewis had written that book twenty years before, in The Problem of Pain, and he had written it as a philosopher. These notebooks were written by a husband, and they are raw.

What the Notebooks Say

In them Lewis records his grief as it happened, day after day. He describes the physical sensations of it: the restlessness, the laziness, the inability to concentrate. He describes the embarrassment of meeting people who did not know what to say, and his own fear of becoming a bore. He describes the way his memories of Joy began, within weeks, to fade and blur, and his terror that he would lose the real woman and be left with an image of his own making.

And he describes, with an honesty that shocked many of his readers, what grief did to his faith. He did not stop believing in God. What frightened him was not that God might not exist, but that God might be other than he had thought: not loving, but cruel. He felt, in the first weeks, that when he turned to God in his need he found a door shut in his face, and silence behind it. He wrote some things about God in those pages that he would not have allowed a pupil to write in an essay. He wrote them because they were what he felt, and because he had decided not to lie.

Then, slowly, the notebooks change. Lewis begins to see that his own frantic demands had been part of the problem: that a man who is shouting cannot hear. He begins to recognise that his picture of God, like his picture of Joy, had been in part his own construction, and that the real God would have to keep breaking it, as the real Joy had broken his picture of her when she was alive. He does not find answers. He finds that the questions themselves begin to look different. And by the end he has come, not to understanding, but to a kind of peace, and a sense that Joy, wherever she was, was at peace with God too.

Published Under Another Name

In time he came to think that the notebooks might help others who were grieving. But the writing was too private to sign, and he did not want it read as the latest offering of a famous Christian author. So he arranged for it to appear under a pseudonym. It appeared in September 1961, published by Faber and Faber, under the name N. W. Clerk, and with the title A Grief Observed. It sold modestly. Very few people knew who had written it.

After Lewis’s death the book was reissued under his own name, and it has since been read by millions of grieving people. Many have said that it was the only book they could bear to read after a death. It has helped them, they say, not because it explains suffering, but because it does not pretend. It shows a Christian of great faith and great intelligence being knocked flat by grief and getting up again, slowly, without having had his questions answered. Readers who have lost someone have found that they are not alone.

The Book and the Man

It is sometimes said that A Grief Observed shows that Lewis lost his faith at the end of his life, or that it undoes the arguments of his earlier books. That is not how he saw it, and it is not what the book itself shows. In the notebooks he goes down into the dark and comes up again. In the months and years that followed he went on praying, going to church, making his Communion and writing about the Christian faith, and his letters of that time are full of a gentle, chastened confidence in God. What the book shows is that faith is not the same as being free from doubt and anguish. It is what remains, and what holds, when doubt and anguish have done their worst.

The Boys

Joy left behind two sons, and Lewis became their guardian. David was sixteen when his mother died, and Douglas fourteen. Both were at boarding school. Lewis, a bachelor of sixty-one who had spent his life among books and adults, now found himself the father of two teenage boys who had just lost their mother.

He did his best, and he did it with great kindness. He paid for their education, gave them a home at the Kilns in the holidays, and treated them with respect. Bill Gresham came to England that summer to see his sons, and Lewis received him courteously. Bill died in 1962.

David, the elder, was a difficult and unhappy young man. In his teens he decided to embrace the Judaism of his mother’s family, and to live as an observant Jew. Lewis, who might have been expected to resist, supported him. He took advice from Jewish scholars in Oxford, helped to arrange for him to learn Hebrew and to keep the Jewish food laws, and made sure he could practise his faith as he wished. Douglas, the younger, was closer to Lewis and to Warnie. He loved the Kilns and its woods, and after Lewis’s death he remained close to Warnie for the rest of Warnie’s life. Many years later he came to a settled Christian faith of his own, and became a writer and a guardian of his stepfather’s literary legacy.

The verse at the head of this chapter is the cry of Psalm 22, which Jesus took on his lips on the cross. It is the prayer of a man who feels abandoned by God, and it is in the Bible. Lewis’s notebooks move in the same direction. He was not given an explanation. He was given, in time, the knowledge that he had been heard.

fields.title: Going Hence
fields.body_html:
“For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.”

— 2 Timothy 4:6-7, KJV

Failing Health

Lewis had always been physically strong. He had walked enormous distances, swum in all weathers and worked long hours for forty years. But after Joy’s death his health began to fail.
