fields.title: The Legacy of C. S. Lewis
fields.body_html:
“And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.”

— Daniel 12:3, KJV

Warnie’s Last Years

Warren Lewis outlived his brother by nine and a half years. They were lonely years. In time he left the Kilns, which under the terms of the original purchase passed to Maureen, and moved to a smaller house nearby in Headington, where a few loyal friends looked after him. He drank, at times heavily, and went back again and again to the nuns at Drogheda, who welcomed him as one of their own. He also did a great deal of useful work. He edited the first collection of his brother’s letters, published in 1966, with a memoir that is still one of the best portraits of Jack. He went on keeping his diary, and in it he wrote, again and again, of how much he missed his brother.

He died on 9 April 1973, and was buried in the same grave as Jack, under the same stone, in the churchyard at Headington Quarry. The two brothers who had invented Boxen in the attic of Little Lea, who had crossed the Irish Sea together in the dark in 1908, and who had shared a house for thirty years, now share a grave.

The Books

When Lewis died, many people assumed that his books would fade. Fashions in religious writing change quickly, and his had been very much the voice of a particular time: of the war years, of the BBC, of an England that was passing. Some critics confidently predicted that he would be forgotten within a generation.

The opposite happened. In the decades after his death his books sold more than they had during his life, and they have never stopped selling. Mere Christianity became one of the most influential Christian books of the century, especially in America, where it has been cited by countless people as the book that led them to faith. The Screwtape Letters and The Problem of Pain remained steadily in print. A Grief Observed, reissued under his own name, found a new readership among the bereaved. The Chronicles of Narnia have been translated into many dozens of languages, adapted for radio, stage, television and film, and read by successive generations of children around the world.

His scholarly work, too, has lasted. The Allegory of Love, his study of Spenser and of the medieval picture of the universe are still read by students of English literature. At Oxford and Cambridge, and in universities across the world, he is now studied as a writer in his own right.

The Man Behind the Books

What kind of man was he? Those who knew him describe a big, ruddy, untidy man with a booming laugh and a prodigious memory, who could quote whole pages of poetry and loved long walks, beer, plain food and good conversation. He disliked fuss, modern gadgets, newspapers and talk about himself. He could be overbearing in argument and was sometimes wounding in his wit. But he was also, by every account, generous to a fault, unfailingly kind to the weak and the troubled, faithful in his friendships, and humble about his own spiritual state.

He was not a saint in any stained-glass sense. He had real faults, and he knew them better than his admirers did. But the long story told in this book is the story of a man in whom God was steadily at work. The arrogant young atheist of the 1920s became, by the end of his life, a man who went to confession every week for twelve years, gave away most of his income, answered thousands of letters from strangers, nursed an old woman through her long decline, married a dying woman and loved her to the end, and faced his own death in peace. That transformation is perhaps the most convincing argument for Christianity that he ever offered.

Poets’ Corner

On 22 November 2013, the fiftieth anniversary of his death, a memorial stone to C. S. Lewis was dedicated in Poets’ Corner in Westminster Abbey, among the memorials to Chaucer, Shakespeare, Milton and the other great writers of the English language. Its inscription, cut in a circle around his name like the rays of a sun, is a sentence from an address he gave to the Socratic Club in 1944, likening the Christian faith to the risen sun, by whose light everything else is seen.

It was a remarkable honour for a man who had been passed over for every professorship in his own university and whose Christian writing many of his colleagues had despised. It came half a century late. Lewis would probably have laughed.

Where He Must Be Weighed

Lewis was loved by evangelicals, and he still is. But he never called himself an evangelical, and on several points his views differed from those of most evangelical readers. He held a high view of Scripture as the Word of God, but not the doctrine of inerrancy. He believed in a purifying purgatory and prayed for the dead. He hoped that some who had never known the name of Christ might yet be saved by him. He made a weekly confession to a priest. These matters belong to his teaching, and they are weighed carefully in the companion volume, Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis. They are mentioned here only so that no reader mistakes this book’s gratitude for an endorsement of everything he believed. Lewis himself would have wanted every claim tested by Scripture, and he would have wanted his readers to follow Christ, not him.

Shining as the Stars

The verse at the head of this chapter is from the book of Daniel: those who turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever. No one can count how many people C. S. Lewis turned to righteousness. Some of them heard him on the radio in 1941. Some read Mere Christianity in a university library in 1970 or 2010. Some met Aslan as children and recognised him, years later, in the Gospels. Some found A Grief Observed on the worst night of their lives. Lewis never knew most of them. He would have said that it was not his doing, and he would have been right. But he was the instrument, and the star shines on.

fields.title: Appendix A: Lessons from the Life of C. S. Lewis
fields.body_html:
“For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.”

— Romans 15:4, KJV

The lessons below gather some of the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. They are not a method, and they are not a portrait of a perfect man. Lewis would have been embarrassed by any attempt to make him a model. They are lessons drawn from the way God dealt with him, and each rests on Scripture rather than on his example alone.

1. God Pursues Those Who Run

Lewis did not find God; he was found. Through years of argument and evasion, God kept closing every exit, until at last the most reluctant of converts knelt down. No one is beyond that pursuit. “I was found of them that sought me not” (Romans 10:20, KJV).

2. Old Wounds Can Be Brought Back to God

Lewis’s unbelief had roots in a child’s unanswered prayer and a mother’s death. He did not pretend that the wound did not matter. In time he brought it back to God, and it became the source of his tenderness to the grieving. “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psalm 147:3, KJV).

3. A Promise Is Worth Keeping

At eighteen, Lewis promised a friend that he would care for his family if he died. He kept that promise for more than thirty years, at great cost, long after anyone would have blamed him for letting it go. “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” shall dwell in God’s holy hill (Psalm 15:4, KJV).

4. The Mind Is Not the Enemy of Faith

Lewis was trained to argue by an atheist, and he never stopped arguing. He came to believe that honest thinking leads towards God, not away from him, and he spent his life giving reasons for his hope. “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD” (Isaiah 1:18, KJV).

5. Friendship Is a Means of Grace

It was in conversation with friends, walking under the trees at Magdalen, that the last barrier to faith came down. For the rest of his life Lewis was sustained by a circle of Christian friends who loved the same things and told each other the truth. “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Proverbs 27:17, KJV).

6. Belong to a Church

Lewis disliked hymns and was not by temperament a joiner. He went to church anyway, every week for thirty years, because he believed that a Christian must belong to the body of Christ. “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Hebrews 10:25, KJV).

7. Confess Your Sins

Fame was a danger to Lewis’s soul, and he knew it. Week after week for twelve years he confessed his sins to an old priest who was not impressed by him. Readers who do not share his practice may still share his humility. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9, KJV).

8. Pray When Prayer Is Dry

Lewis prayed every day for decades, often without feeling anything, and he prayed by name for people he had never met. He had learned as a boy that feelings are a poor measure of prayer. “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17, KJV).

9. Give Freely

Lewis put two-thirds of his royalties into a trust for the poor and gave away much of the rest. He lived simply and did not want to grow rich on the gospel. “Freely ye have received, freely give” (Matthew 10:8, KJV).

10. Serve the Ones Who Write to You

Lewis answered thousands of letters from strangers, by hand, for more than twenty years. It was dull, exhausting and unseen work, and he did it as a duty to Christ. “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Matthew 25:40, KJV).

11. Take Criticism Honestly

When a young philosopher showed that one of his arguments was flawed, Lewis was hurt, but he went back to his desk and rewrote it. A Christian need not fear the truth, even when it is unwelcome. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6, KJV).

12. Love Late, and Love Fully

Lewis married a dying woman in a hospital room and loved her to the end. He did not hold back his heart for fear of losing her, though he knew that he would. “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it” (Song of Solomon 8:7, KJV).

13. Grief Is Not Unbelief

When Joy died, Lewis did not hide his anguish or his doubts. He wrote them down, and in the end he came through them. A Christian may cry out to God in the dark, as the psalmists and Christ himself did. “Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD” (Psalm 130:1, KJV).

14. Die Ready

Lewis faced his death calmly and without fear, having lived for thirty years in the faith he had once resisted. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21, KJV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”

— James 1:22, KJV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty weeks. Its purpose is not to make C. S. Lewis an object of admiration, but to let his life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Those who want to go further are encouraged to read Lewis’s own books, obtained from their publishers or a library, alongside these chapters.

Chapter 1 - Little Lea

Central idea

A bookish Belfast childhood, a close brother and a house full of books gave Lewis the materials of his imagination, and a longing he could not name.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 22:6; Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Psalm 16:6.

Reflection

1. What did your childhood give you that God has since used? 2. Is there a longing in you that nothing on earth has satisfied?

Chapter 2 - August 1908

Central idea

A mother’s death, a prayer that seemed unanswered, and a father lost in grief sent a nine-year-old into the world alone.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 27:10; Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 49:15.

Reflection

1. Is there an old disappointment with God you have never brought back to him? 2. Whom do you know who is grieving as a child?

Chapter 3 - Schools, and a Faith Let Go

Central idea

Anxious, feelings-centred prayer and a vague spirituality loosened a boy’s faith; a cruel school culture taught him the misery of the inner ring.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 14:1; Matthew 6:7-8; James 4:6.

Reflection

1. Do you measure your prayers by your feelings? 2. Where are you tempted to seek the approval of the “right people”?

Chapter 4 - The Great Knock

Central idea

An atheist tutor sharpened the mind God would later use, and a book bought at a station touched an imagination that reason had not yet reached.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 27:17; Isaiah 45:4-5; Philippians 4:8.

Reflection

1. Who has sharpened your thinking, whether believer or not? 2. What beauty has pointed you towards God before you understood it?

Chapter 5 - A Promise at Keble

Central idea

Two young soldiers made a pact to care for each other’s families, and one of them kept it for more than thirty years.

Scriptures to revisit

Ecclesiastes 5:4-5; Psalm 15:4; Matthew 5:37.

Reflection

1. What promises have you made that you are tempted to let slip? 2. What would it cost you to keep them?

Chapter 6 - 15 April 1918

Central idea

The war wounded Lewis, killed the sergeant beside him and took his friend, and he survived without knowing why.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 91; Psalm 31:15; Romans 8:28.

Reflection

1. When have you been spared something others were not? 2. How do you understand God’s purposes in that?

Chapter 7 - Mrs Moore

Central idea

A young atheist took in a bereaved mother and her daughter and served them for three decades, in a household that was never easy and never fully explained.

Scriptures to revisit

James 1:27; Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 4:25.

Reflection

1. Is there anyone from whom you hide the truth of your life? 2. Whom has God given you to serve at home?

Chapter 8 - Three Firsts and a Fellowship

Central idea

Hard work and lean years made Lewis a scholar, and friendships with Barfield, Coghill and Tolkien began to unsettle his unbelief.

Scriptures to revisit

Colossians 3:23; Ecclesiastes 9:10; Proverbs 13:20.

Reflection

1. For whom do you do your work? 2. Which of your friends challenge you most?

Chapter 9 - Hunted

Central idea

God closed every exit; a father’s death and a son’s regret came before a reluctant surrender to belief in God.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 139:1-12; Jonah 1:1-3; Luke 15:17-20.

Reflection

1. Have you ever felt pursued by God? 2. Is there anyone you wronged who can no longer be put right, and have you brought that to God?

Chapter 10 - Addison’s Walk

Central idea

A night conversation about myth, and a quiet ride in a sidecar, brought Lewis from belief in God to faith in Christ.

Scriptures to revisit

John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Luke 24:13-32.

Reflection

1. How did you come to faith in Christ, not merely belief in God? 2. Whom has God used to remove barriers to faith for you?

Chapter 11 - The Kilns

Central idea

A strange household on the edge of Oxford, a faithful parish church and a first Christian book: the shape of a converted life.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 127:1; Hebrews 10:24-25; Acts 2:42.

Reflection

1. Do you belong to a local church, even when it does not suit your tastes? 2. Who is God building into your household?

Chapter 12 - Thursday Evenings

Central idea

The Inklings met to read their work and talk about the things of God, and Charles Williams’s friendship and death marked Lewis deeply.

Scriptures to revisit

Malachi 3:16; Proverbs 18:24; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14.

Reflection

1. Do you have friends with whom you can speak of God honestly? 2. How might you be such a friend?

Chapter 13 - A Voice on the Wireless

Central idea

In war Lewis wrote of pain, invented a devil’s letters, spoke on the BBC and learned humility talking to airmen.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Peter 3:15; Colossians 4:6; 1 Corinthians 9:22.

Reflection

1. Could you explain your faith plainly to a neighbour? 2. What would you need to drop to be understood?

Chapter 14 - A Rule of Life

Central idea

Confession, disciplined prayer, a trust for the poor and the daily burden of letters guarded Lewis against the dangers of fame.

Scriptures to revisit

James 5:16; Matthew 6:1-6; 2 Corinthians 9:7.

Reflection

1. Who knows the worst about you? 2. What is your rule of prayer and giving?

Chapter 15 - The Socratic Club

Central idea

Lewis welcomed the strongest objections to his faith, and when he was answered well he revised his work rather than abandoning it.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Thessalonians 5:21; Proverbs 18:17; Acts 17:11.

Reflection

1. How do you respond when an argument you trust is shown to be weak? 2. Are you afraid of hard questions?

Chapter 16 - The Long Decline

Central idea

An old woman’s decline, a brother’s drinking and professional slights tested Lewis’s patience and nearly broke his health.

Scriptures to revisit

Galatians 6:2; 1 Corinthians 13:4-7; 1 Peter 5:6.

Reflection

1. Whose burden are you carrying, unseen? 2. How do you respond when others are honoured and you are passed over?

Chapter 17 - A Wardrobe and a Chair

Central idea

A scholar in his fifties wrote for children, and Cambridge gave him the recognition Oxford had withheld.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 18:3; Mark 10:14-15; Psalm 8:2.

Reflection

1. What would it mean for you to receive the kingdom as a child? 2. How do you speak of God to children?

Chapter 18 - Joy Davidman

Central idea

A former Communist from New York, converted in a night of helplessness, became Lewis’s friend and, by a legal formality, his wife.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 71:5; Psalm 46:1; 2 Corinthians 5:17.

Reflection

1. What brought you to the end of your own strength? 2. Whom has God brought into your life unexpectedly?

Chapter 19 - A Bedside Wedding

Central idea

Faced with Joy’s cancer, Lewis discovered he loved her; a priest married them at her bedside and prayed for her healing.

Scriptures to revisit

James 5:14-15; Ruth 1:16-17; Colossians 1:24.

Reflection

1. Have you ever been willing to love at great cost? 2. How do you pray for the sick?

Chapter 20 - Three Years

Central idea

A late and unexpected happiness, a journey to Greece and the return of the cancer: a time to dance, and then a time to weep.

Scriptures to revisit

Ecclesiastes 3:1-8; Psalm 90:12; Song of Solomon 8:6-7.

Reflection

1. Are you receiving today’s gifts as gifts? 2. How would you spend three years if you knew that was all you had?

Chapter 21 - A Grief Observed

Central idea

Lewis wrote his grief down without disguise, went down into the dark, and came up again with no answers but a renewed trust.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 22; Psalm 88; Lamentations 3:19-26.

Reflection

1. Have you allowed yourself to grieve honestly before God? 2. How can you sit with someone who is grieving without pretending?

Chapter 22 - Going Hence

Central idea

Illness, a coma, resignation and a quiet death at home, with a brother who loved him and a faith that held.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Timothy 4:6-8; John 11:25-26; Philippians 1:21-23.

Reflection

1. How do you think about your own death? 2. What would you want to have kept?

Chapter 23 - The Legacy of C. S. Lewis

Central idea

His books, his transformed character and a memorial in Westminster Abbey, together with the places where his teaching must be weighed.

Scriptures to revisit

Daniel 12:3; 1 Corinthians 3:5-7; Hebrews 13:7.

Reflection

1. Whose faith have you been asked to follow, and how do you test it? 2. To whom might God use you to point the way?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of C. S. Lewis
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, KJV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Where the sources disagree, the disagreement is noted.

1895 - Warren

Warren Hamilton Lewis is born in Belfast on 16 June, the elder son of Albert James Lewis, a solicitor, and Florence (Flora) Hamilton Lewis.

1898 - Jack

Clive Staples Lewis is born on 29 November at Dundela Villas, Strandtown, Belfast. As a small boy he takes the name Jacksie, later Jack.

1905 - Little Lea

In April the family moves to Little Lea, a new house on the Circular Road, Strandtown. Warnie goes to Wynyard School, Watford.

1908 - His Mother’s Death

Flora Lewis dies of cancer on 23 August. In September Jack is sent to Wynyard School with Warnie.

1910-1913 - Schools

Wynyard closes in 1910. Jack spends a term at Campbell College, Belfast, then from January 1911 attends Cherbourg House, Malvern, where he abandons the Christian faith.

1913-1914 - Malvern College

Jack attends Malvern College from September 1913 to the summer of 1914. In April 1914 he meets Arthur Greeves.

1914-1917 - Great Bookham

From September 1914 Jack is tutored by William T. Kirkpatrick at Great Bookham, Surrey. He is confirmed at St Mark’s, Dundela, in December 1914, without belief.

1916 - Phantastes

In March he buys George MacDonald’s Phantastes at Leatherhead station. In December he wins a scholarship to University College, Oxford.

1917 - Oxford and the Army

He comes up to University College in April. In June he joins a cadet battalion at Keble College and shares a room with Paddy Moore. Commissioned in the Somerset Light Infantry in September, he reaches the front line in France on his nineteenth birthday, 29 November.

1918 - Wounded

Paddy Moore is posted missing in late March and later confirmed killed. On 15 April Lewis is wounded at Mont-Bernenchon, and Sergeant Harry Ayres is killed beside him. He convalesces in England and is demobilised in December.

1919 - Return to Oxford

Lewis resumes his studies in January. Mrs Moore and Maureen settle in Oxford. Spirits in Bondage is published in March under the name Clive Hamilton.

1920-1923 - Three Firsts

First Class in Honour Moderations (1920), Literae Humaniores (1922) and English (1923).

1925 - Magdalen

In May Lewis is elected a Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, as tutor in English.

1926 - Tolkien

On 11 May Lewis meets J. R. R. Tolkien at a meeting of the English faculty at Merton College.

1929 - His Father’s Death

Albert Lewis dies in Belfast on 25 September.

1929 or 1930 - Theism

Lewis kneels and acknowledges God in his rooms at Magdalen. He dates it to the summer term of 1929; Alister McGrath has argued, and most scholars now accept, that it was the summer term of 1930.

1930 - The Kilns

On 10 October Lewis, Mrs Moore and Maureen move into the Kilns, Headington Quarry.

1931 - Faith in Christ

On 19 September Lewis talks through the night with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson on Addison’s Walk. On 28 September, on the way to Whipsnade Zoo, he comes to believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. On Christmas Day he takes Communion at Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry.

1932-1933 - The Pilgrim’s Regress

Warnie retires from the army in December 1932 and makes his home at the Kilns. The Pilgrim’s Regress is published in 1933.

1936-1938 - Scholar and Novelist

The Allegory of Love (1936). Friendship with Charles Williams begins. Out of the Silent Planet (1938).

1939 - War

Evacuee children come to the Kilns. Charles Williams moves to Oxford with the Oxford University Press.

1940 - Pain and Confession

The Problem of Pain is published in October. In the same month Lewis begins weekly confession with Father Walter Adams of the Society of St John the Evangelist.

1941 - Screwtape and the BBC

The Screwtape Letters appear weekly in The Guardian from May to November. Lewis begins speaking to the RAF. His first BBC talk is broadcast on 6 August. He preaches The Weight of Glory on 8 June.

1942 - The Socratic Club

The Socratic Club holds its first meeting in January, with Lewis as president. The Screwtape Letters is published as a book in February. Around this time the Agape Fund is set up.

1943-1945 - The War Years

The Abolition of Man (1943), Perelandra (1943), the last of the broadcast talks (1944), That Hideous Strength and The Great Divorce (1945). Charles Williams dies on 15 May 1945.

1947 - Miracles

Miracles is published. Lewis appears on the cover of Time in September. Warnie is treated at Drogheda.

1948 - Anscombe

On 2 February Elizabeth Anscombe reads her criticism of Miracles to the Socratic Club. Lewis later revises the chapter for the 1960 edition.

1949 - Exhaustion

In June Lewis collapses and is treated in the Acland nursing home.

1950 - Narnia

In January Joy Davidman first writes to Lewis. In April Mrs Moore enters Restholme nursing home. The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe is published in October.

1951 - Mrs Moore’s Death

Janie Moore dies on 12 January and is buried at Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry.

1952 - Meeting Joy

Mere Christianity is published. Father Walter Adams dies. On 24 September Lewis meets Joy Davidman at the Eastgate Hotel, Oxford.

1954-1955 - Cambridge

Lewis accepts the new chair of Medieval and Renaissance English at Cambridge, gives his inaugural lecture on 29 November 1954, and takes up residence at Magdalene College in January 1955. Surprised by Joy is published in 1955.

1956 - Marriage and Cancer

The Last Battle, the seventh Narnia book, and Till We Have Faces are published. On 23 April Lewis and Joy marry in a civil ceremony at the Oxford register office. On 18 October Joy’s femur breaks and cancer is diagnosed.

1957 - The Bedside Wedding

On 21 March Peter Bide marries Lewis and Joy in her hospital room and prays for her healing. Joy goes home to the Kilns and her cancer goes into remission. Lewis develops osteoporosis.

1958-1959 - Three Years

Reflections on the Psalms (1958). A honeymoon in Ireland (1958). In October 1959 Joy’s cancer returns.

1960 - Greece and Joy’s Death

The Four Loves is published. From 3 to 14 April Lewis and Joy tour Greece with Roger and June Lancelyn Green. Joy dies at the Radcliffe Infirmary on 13 July. Lewis becomes guardian of David and Douglas Gresham.

1961 - A Grief Observed

A Grief Observed is published in September under the name N. W. Clerk. Lewis falls seriously ill and misses the autumn term.

1963 - Going Hence

On 15 July Lewis suffers a heart attack and falls into a coma; he receives the last rites on 16 July and wakes. He resigns his Cambridge chair in August. He dies at the Kilns on 22 November, a week before his sixty-fifth birthday, and is buried at Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry, on 26 November.

1964 - Posthumous Books

Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer and The Discarded Image are published.

1973 - Warnie

Warren Lewis dies on 9 April and is buried in his brother’s grave.

2013 - Poets’ Corner

On 22 November, the fiftieth anniversary of his death, a memorial to C. S. Lewis is dedicated in Poets’ Corner, Westminster Abbey.

Warnie is treated at Drogheda. 1948 - Anscombe On 2 February Elizabeth Anscombe reads her criticism of Miracles to the Socratic Club. Lewis later revises the chapter for the 1960 edition. 1949 - Exhaustion In June Lewis collapses and is treated in the Acland nursing home. 1950 - Narnia In January Joy Davidman first writes to Lewis. In April Mrs Moore enters Restholme nursing home. The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe is published in October. 1951 - Mrs Moore’s Death Janie Moore dies on 12 January and is buried at Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry. 1952 - Meeting Joy Mere Christianity is published. Father Walter Adams dies. On 24 September Lewis meets Joy Davidman at the Eastgate Hotel, Oxford. 1954-1955 - Cambridge Lewis accepts the new chair of Medieval and Renaissance English at Cambridge, gives his inaugural lecture on 29 November 1954, and takes up residence at Magdalene College in January 1955. Surprised by Joy is published in 1955. 1956 - Marriage and Cancer The Last Battle, the seventh Narnia book, and Till We Have Faces are published. On 23 April Lewis and Joy marry in a civil ceremony at the Oxford register office. On 18 October Joy’s femur breaks and cancer is diagnosed. 1957 - The Bedside Wedding On 21 March Peter Bide marries Lewis and Joy in her hospital room and prays for her healing. Joy goes home to the Kilns and her cancer goes into remission. Lewis develops osteoporosis. 1958-1959 - Three Years Reflections on the Psalms (1958). A honeymoon in Ireland (1958). In October 1959 Joy’s cancer returns. 1960 - Greece and Joy’s Death The Four Loves is published. From 3 to 14 April Lewis and Joy tour Greece with Roger and June Lancelyn Green. Joy dies at the Radcliffe Infirmary on 13 July. Lewis becomes guardian of David and Douglas Gresham. 1961 - A Grief Observed A Grief Observed is published in September under the name N. W. Clerk. Lewis falls seriously ill and misses the autumn term. 1963 - Going Hence On 15 July Lewis suffers a heart attack and falls into a coma; he receives the last rites on 16 July and wakes. He resigns his Cambridge chair in August. He dies at the Kilns on 22 November, a week before his sixty-fifth birthday, and is buried at Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry, on 26 November. 1964 - Posthumous Books Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer and The Discarded Image are published. 1973 - Warnie Warren Lewis dies on 9 April and is buried in his brother’s grave. 2013 - Poets’ Corner On 22 November, the fiftieth anniversary of his death, a memorial to C. S. Lewis is dedicated in Poets’ Corner, Westminster Abbey.

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”

— 1 Thessalonians 5:21, KJV

About This Work

This book is an independent biography written by Ochorus. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by the C. S. Lewis estate, or by any publisher, company or organisation that holds rights in the writings of C. S. Lewis. Lewis’s books, letters and other writings remain in copyright, and they should be obtained from their publishers or borrowed from a library. Readers are warmly encouraged to do so.

The book tells his life in its own words. It quotes Lewis directly only three times, each in a single short sentence from a published book:

Surprised by Joy (1955), chapter 14. His description of himself, on the night he acknowledged God, as “the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.”

Surprised by Joy (1955), chapter 15. His account of the ride to Whipsnade: “When we set out I did not believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and when we reached the zoo I did.”

A Grief Observed (1961), opening sentence. “No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear.”

Everything else attributed to Lewis, whether from his books, his letters or the memories of others, is paraphrased. The only other words quoted are those of Scripture and one line of Shakespeare, from King Lear, which is in the public domain. No letter, poem or story of Lewis’s is reproduced, and the plots of his stories are mentioned only in a sentence where the life requires it.

Primary Sources

Lewis’s own account of his early life is Surprised by Joy: The Shape of My Early Life (1955). His diary for 1922 to 1927 was published as All My Road Before Me (1991). His letters were collected and edited by Walter Hooper as The Collected Letters of C. S. Lewis (three volumes, 2000 to 2006), and his letters to Arthur Greeves had earlier appeared as They Stand Together (1979). Warren Lewis’s memoir of his brother was printed in Letters of C. S. Lewis (1966), and a selection from his diaries was published as Brothers and Friends (1982). Joy Davidman’s letters were collected in Out of My Bone (2009). Her account of her conversion appeared in the collection These Found the Way (1951).

Biographies and Studies

This book is particularly indebted to the following, which readers who want to go further will find rewarding:

Roger Lancelyn Green and Walter Hooper, C. S. Lewis: A Biography (1974; revised 2002). The first full life, written by two friends.

George Sayer, Jack: C. S. Lewis and His Times (1988; revised 1994). The portrait of a former pupil and close friend.

Alan Jacobs, The Narnian: The Life and Imagination of C. S. Lewis (2005). A sympathetic study of the man and his imagination.

Alister McGrath, C. S. Lewis: A Life: Eccentric Genius, Reluctant Prophet (2013). A biography based on a fresh reading of the letters, which revised the date of his conversion to theism.

Philip and Carol Zaleski, The Fellowship: The Literary Lives of the Inklings (2015). Lewis among Tolkien, Barfield and Williams.

Also consulted: A. N. Wilson, C. S. Lewis: A Biography (1990); Lyle W. Dorsett, And God Came In (1983) and Abigail Santamaria, Joy: Poet, Seeker, and the Woman Who Captivated C. S. Lewis (2015), on Joy Davidman; Douglas Gresham, Lenten Lands (1988), a stepson’s memoir; and Humphrey Carpenter, The Inklings (1978).

Corrections and Disputed Points

The date of his conversion to theism. Lewis gave the summer term of 1929. This book follows McGrath and most later scholars in preferring the summer of 1930, which places it after his father’s death, while noting that some still defend 1929.

The ride to Whipsnade. Most accounts date it to 28 September 1931, nine days after the night on Addison’s Walk. A few give an earlier date in the same month.

Janie Moore. Whether Lewis and Mrs Moore were lovers in the early years is disputed. Wilson and McGrath think it likely, and Sayer came to think so; Hooper and others denied it. Lewis never explained the relationship, and no document settles it. This book does not claim to know.

The Anscombe debate. The story that Lewis was so humiliated by Elizabeth Anscombe in 1948 that he gave up apologetics is not supported by the evidence. He revised the chapter she criticised and went on writing Christian books of many kinds; Anscombe herself rejected the legend.

The marriage. Films and plays, especially Shadowlands, have changed the ages of Joy’s sons, left one of them out, and invented scenes. The account here follows the letters, Warnie’s diaries and the biographies.

Quotations attributed to Lewis. Many sayings circulated under his name are not his. Readers who wish to quote him should check the words against his own books.

The Library He Loved

Lewis believed that every reader should go back to the old books, and many of the writers who shaped his faith are in the public domain and in the Ochorus library. Athanasius’s On the Incarnation was a book he loved and commended to others. Augustine’s Confessions is the great ancestor of every story of a reluctant convert, including his own. John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress gave him the pattern for his first Christian book. Thomas à Kempis’s The Imitation of Christ was among the devotional books he read for years. And William Law’s A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life was a book he valued for its searching seriousness. All of these can be read freely on Ochorus, alongside the companion volume Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis.

Scripture

All Scripture quotations are from the Authorised (King James) Version, which is in the public domain.
